articles.title: US to blacklist Asian AI firm Megaspeed after Nvidia scandal
articles.summary: Megaspeed has been accused of funneling AI chips to China after a former executive's affair with Jensen Huang became public.
articles.body:
The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.

The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.

The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.

Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.

Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.

China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.

On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".

The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.

The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.

China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.

Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.

Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.

Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.

Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.

That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.

Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.

Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.

Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .

The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.

In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.

Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

articles.title: Patxi López alerta sobre el retroceso democrático y contesta a Rufián tras sus quejas: "El Gobierno no encarcela a nadie"
articles.standfirst: Los portavoces de PSOE y ERC hablaron sobre memoria histórica y justicia
articles.summary: Los portavoces de PSOE y ERC hablaron sobre memoria histórica y justicia
articles.body: El debate a ocho celebrado en RTVE durante la intervención del portavoz socialista, Patxi López, alertó sobre el avance de los discursos autoritarios y las consecuencias de los pactos entre la derecha y la ultraderecha. El dirigente del PSOE inició su alegato de forma contundente al señalar el auge de sectores extremistas: "Nazis. Han alimentado a los que dicen que prefieren una dictadura a una democracia, a los que dicen que con Franco se vivía mejor y lo peor es que ya empiezan a aplicar políticas de esos tiempos allí donde gobiernan". A lo largo de su exposición, López enumeró lo que considera un retroceso en derechos y libertades en las instituciones lideradas por ambas formaciones conservadoras. "Y en este país ha vuelto la censura a la cultura en algunos sitios donde gobierna el PP y Vox. Y en este país algunos han llamado basura, algunas, a los sindicatos", afirmó el portavoz socialista. Tras denunciar que "se cargan las leyes de memoria", lamentó que "como niegan la violencia machista y como niegan la emergencia climática, se están cargando todo lo que tanto nos ha costado eh conquistar en este país", concluyendo con un llamamiento a las urnas: "Bueno, pues el día 29 también se vota en defensa propia, en contra de esto". Sin embargo, el turno de palabra derivó en un enfrentamiento directo cuando el portavoz de Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya, Gabriel Rufián, interrumpió al diputado socialista para exigir responsabilidades sobre la presencia de grupos ultras en el espacio público. "Patxi, es ilegal también que fascistas se paseen por la calle. Hay una ley de memoria...", reprochó Rufián en referencia a recientes marchas de carácter ultraderechista. Ante esta interpelación, López eludió la responsabilidad del Ejecutivo y señaló directamente al poder judicial: "Pregúntaselo al juez que permitió la manifestación". El intercambio subió de tono cuando el dirigente republicano insistió en el cumplimiento de la normativa vigente y sacó a relucir las condenas a sindicalistas ocurridas durante el mandato actual. "Bueno, pero hay una ley de memoria histórica aprobada y es ilegal, y hay tres chavales en la trena por defender la huelga general de derechos de trabajadores con un gobierno del PSOE que todavía están ahí", argumentó Rufián. El portavoz socialista replicó de inmediato para marcar distancias respecto a las decisiones judiciales: "No, pero el gobierno no encarcela a nadie. Encarcelan algunos jueces, Gabriel". Lejos de dar por zanjada la discusión, Rufián reiteró su acusación vinculando los encarcelamientos con la etapa del actual Ejecutivo: "Bueno, con este gobierno hay tres chavales en la trena por defender los derechos...". Finalmente, Patxi López cerró el cruce de reproches manteniendo su postura sobre la separación de poderes y negando cualquier implicación gubernamental en dichas penas de prisión con una última réplica: "No, pero el gobierno no encarcela a nadie", le volvió a recordar.

articles.title: Trump and Newsom clash over California death penalty and presidential pardons
articles.summary: Trump in Washington: Newsom is granting clemency to child killers. Newsom on video: Trump sells mercy.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump and Gov. Gavin Newsom traded barbs on Monday over Newsom's plan to commute the death sentences of more than 500 condemned California inmates to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

The dueling statements, in which each accused the other of allowing criminals to walk free, came as crime victims and prosecutors who support the death penalty met with Trump in Washington, D.C. and joined him at a news conference.

They are the latest public airing of the Trump administration's rancorous relationship with California. Trump's Department of Justice has sued the state numerous times, recently seeking to force its majority Democratic leaders to set aside ballots from 20,000 voters the government said might not be U.S. citizens. California, in turn, has sued the federal government more than 100 times in less than two years.

"Just days ago the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, granted clemency and mercy to 548 of the most evil monsters on the face of the earth," Trump said. "Among those death row inmates he granted clemency were more than 110 child killers, more than 100 rapists who murdered their victims, and numerous serial killers who tortured and slaughtered dozens of innocent people."

Sitting in a row of chairs alongside him were victims rights advocates including Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was abducted from her Petaluma home and murdered in 1993, and Sandy Friend, whose 8-year-old son Michael Lyons was kidnapped in Yuba City in 1996, sexually assaulted and stabbed to death.

Newsom releases video about Trump's pardons

But Newsom, who announced his plan to commute the death sentences on Nov. 5 but has not yet done so, anticipated the president's remarks, releasing a video in advance of the news conference listing pardons granted by Trump to wealthy supporters.

Trump, Newsom said in his video, took out full page ads in local newspapers calling for the death penalty for five men, later determined via DNA testing to be innocent, convicted of attacking a jogger in New York's Central Park in 1989.

Trump refused to apologize after they were exonerated, Newsom said, yet as president granted pardons to convicted swindlers and others who gave money to his campaigns.

"Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy — he sells it," Newsom said, appearing in front of the U.S. and California flags. "If you're poor, black or brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."

articles.title: Após Câmara aprovar ajuste fiscal, Motta defende novas medidas em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente da Câmara disse que projeto aprovado nesta segunda dará condições para Lula adequar Orçamento de 2027 e que espera ações para um ambiente econômico "mais saudável".
articles.summary: Hugo Motta defende novas medidas econômicas após a Câmara aprovar o ajuste fiscal de Lula, visando reduzir o dólar e garantir um cenário saudável para 2027.
articles.body:
O presidente da Câmara dos Deputados , Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), defendeu nesta segunda-feira (23) que o governo do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) adote novas medidas na economia ainda em 2026.

"Eu espero [...] que o governo possa se conscientizar de que é necessário, ainda nesse ano, tomarmos mais algumas medidas no que diz respeito à economia do país", afirmou Hugo Motta durante a votação da proposta do governo.

Segundo ele, as eventuais medidas não devem prejudicar a população mais pobre nem comprometer políticas consideradas prioritárias pelo presidente.

"Eu não estou aqui defendendo que prejudiquemos os mais pobres ou que o presidente abra mão daquilo que é para ele um pilar de sustentação da sua trajetória política, mas que tenhamos condições de ter um ambiente econômico mais saudável, com a queda na taxa de juros", declarou.

Ao defender novas medidas, Hugo Motta também mencionou a alta do dólar e seus efeitos sobre a inflação e a população de menor renda.

"Infelizmente, o que vimos acontecer foi a alta do preço do dólar. Isso impacta diretamente na inflação, prejudica os que mais precisam e tira aquilo que é mais importante para todos nós, que é proteger as pessoas mais carentes", disse.

Para o presidente da Câmara, as novas medidas permitiriam que o país começasse 2027 em um cenário econômico diferente.

"Nós precisamos fazer um ajuste econômico importante, quem sabe ainda nesse ano, para que o Brasil entre o ano 2027 com um novo cenário", afirmou.

Motta disse ainda que o ajuste fiscal foi aprovado com apoio de partidos de centro, que classificou como "fundamentais" para o resultado. O presidente da Câmara afirmou que vai trabalhar para consolidar uma base de apoio ao governo Lula entre estes partidos.

O presidente da República, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT)(e), e o presidente da Câmara dos Deputados, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), durante a cerimônia de assinatura da medida provisória da reforma do setor elétrico, no Palácio do Planalto, em Brasília (DF), em 21 de maio de 2025. — Foto: Wilton Junior/Estadão Conteúdo

Os deputados aprovarem o projeto de ajuste fiscal enviado pelo governo na noite desta segunda. O texto-base recebeu 353 votos favoráveis, 128 contrários e cinco abstenções.

A proposta prevê medidas para reduzir despesas e ampliar receitas e busca permitir o cumprimento da meta prevista no Orçamento de 2027.

Segundo estimativa do Ministério do Planejamento, as medidas podem representar um impacto de até R$ 56 bilhões nas contas públicas no próximo ano.

Entre os pontos do projeto estão um novo corte de 10% em incentivos e benefícios tributários e mudanças nas despesas discricionárias. O texto também permite que o Executivo limite o uso de créditos tributários de empresas para compensar impostos devidos à Receita Federal.

Hugo Motta decidiu acelerar a análise da proposta na Câmara e convocou sessão para esta segunda, dia em que normalmente não há votações no plenário.

Segundo o presidente da Casa, a decisão ocorreu diante da preocupação do Congresso com a alta do dólar e com a perspectiva de juros elevados.

articles.title: Cidadania, de passado comunista, vive racha sobre incorporação ao PP | G1
articles.standfirst: Roberto Freire, que integrou o antigo Partido Comunista Brasileiro e fundou o PPS, depois transformado no Cidadania, considera que a incorporação ao PP seria uma "violência". Em jogo estão a formação de bancadas no Congresso e a distribuição do Fundo Partidário.
articles.summary: A incorporação do Cidadania ao PP gerou um racha interno e o adiamento da votação após Roberto Freire criticar a união entre herdeiros do PCB e da Arena.
articles.body:
Alex Manente e Roberto Freire, integrantes do Cidadania — Foto: Thiago Cristino/Câmara dos Deputados; Reprodução/Instagram

O Cidadania vive um impasse e está dividido sobre uma possível incorporação pelo Progressistas (PP), um dos maiores partidos do Congresso. O movimento extinguiria o Cidadania, cujas origens estão ligadas ao antigo Partido Comunista Brasileiro (PCB). Já o PP é descendente da Arena, o partido criado pela ditadura militar nos anos 1960 para representar o regime.

Em jogo estão a composição de bancadas no Congresso e a distribuição do Fundo Partidário, dinheiro público que ajuda a manter o funcionamento das legendas.

Um congresso que seria realizado no último fim de semana para discutir o futuro do Cidadania foi adiado em meio às divergências. O deputado federal Alex Manente (SP), presidente da sigla, afirmou nesta segunda-feira (23) que a discussão será ampliada para envolver outras lideranças.

"Foi por isso que suspendemos o Congresso antes da votação. Seguimos conversando com outros partidos, e eventuais definições sobre diretórios, eleitos e fundação passarão pelas instâncias partidárias", disse Manente ao g1 .

Em paralelo, o ministro Cristiano Zanin, do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), concedeu uma liminar para suspender o congresso do Cidadania. Ele atendeu ao pedido de uma ala do partido.

O ex-deputado e ex-senador Roberto Freire, que disputou a Presidência em 1989 pelo PCB e depois transformou a sigla no Partido Popular Socialista (PPS), antigo nome do Cidadania, é contra a incorporação pelo PP.

Desde 2022, o Cidadania forma uma federação com o PSDB. Nesse modelo, os partidos devem atuar juntos, como se fossem um só, por pelo menos quatro anos. A federação é diferente da coligação, que vale apenas para períodos eleitorais.

Juntos, Cidadania e PSDB superaram a cláusula de desempenho nas eleições deste ano, mas devido aos resultados do PSDB, que elegeu 11 deputados federais e dois senadores. Com isso, mantêm acesso ao Fundo Partidário.

Em março, o Cidadania havia decidido deixar a federação , mas o rompimento ainda não foi formalizado.

Enquanto o impasse permanece, o PSDB negocia uma aliança com o MDB. Uma das possibilidades seria substituir o Cidadania pelo MDB na federação para os próximos anos.

Roberto Freire defende manter a federação com o PSDB e discutir a entrada do MDB como terceiro elemento. Para ele, incorporar o Cidadania ao PP, considerando as trajetórias de antagonismo dos dois partidos, seria uma violência.

“Ele [Alex Manente] percebeu que foi uma violência tão grande que voltou atrás. Se ele quer mudar de partido, ir para o Progressistas, pode ir. O próprio Cidadania deve facilitar a ida e garantir que ele vá com todos os direitos que ele pode ter”, afirmou ao g1 .

Se a federação PSDB-Cidadania for desfeita, o TSE teria que refazer o cálculo para distribuir o Fundo Partidário. O Cidadania não elegeu nem deputados federais nem senadores. Se dependesse apenas de seus resultados, o partido passaria longe de atingir a cláusula de barreira.

Tanto Alex Manente quanto Roberto Freire foram candidatos a deputado federal, e nenhum dos dois se elegeu.

O PP, por sua vez, integra uma federação com o União Brasil e tem uma das maiores bancadas do Congresso. Neste ano, elegeu 41 deputados e seis senadores. Em 2025, o PP recebeu R$ 71,2 milhões do fundo partidário, e o União Brasil, R$ 107,1 milhões. O Cidadania teve direito a R$ 14,9 milhões.

A incorporação pelo PP extinguiria o Cidadania, ex-PPS, sigla criada na década de 1990 sob a liderança de Roberto Freire a partir do PCB.

Atualmente, uma outra versão do PCB tem registro vigente no TSE, sob o comando de Edmilson Costa, que foi candidato à Presidência e teve 22,6 mil votos (0,02% do total).

O PCB foi fundado em 1922, sob influência da revolução de 1917 que levou os bolcheviques ao poder na Rússia, e teve entre seus quadros o escritor Jorge Amado e o militar e líder comunista Luiz Carlos Prestes.

Passou períodos na clandestinidade e, nos anos 1960, uma ala dissidente saiu do PCB para fundar o PC do B, que hoje faz parte de uma federação com PT e PV.

Já o PPS ganhou projeção nacional com as candidaturas de Ciro Gomes à Presidência da República em 1998 e 2002. No segundo turno de 2002, apoiou Lula e, no início do governo, integrou a base aliada. O partido rompeu com a gestão petista em 2004. Ciro permaneceu à frente do Ministério da Integração Nacional, mas foi excluído dos debates internos do partido.

Em 2016, Roberto Freire se tornou ministro da Cultura de Michel Temer (MDB), após o impeachment de Dilma Rousseff (PT). Em 2019, o TSE aprovou a mudança do nome do PPS para Cidadania. O partido abandonou bandeiras associadas ao socialismo e adotou o liberalismo econômico.

Já a trajetória do PP passa pelo Partido Democrático Social (PDS), que sucedeu a Arena após o fim do bipartidarismo que tinha o MDB como força de oposição aos militares.

Em 1993, o PDS se fundiu com o Partido Democrata Cristão (PDC) e deu origem ao Partido Progressista Reformador (PPR). Dois anos depois, o PPR se uniu a outra legenda, então chamada Partido Progressista, para formar o Partido Progressista Brasileiro (PPB), que deu origem ao atual Progressistas.

A discussão sobre a incorporação se somou a uma disputa pelo comando do Cidadania que já tramitava na Justiça. O ex-deputado estadual Comte Bittencourt (RJ) assumiu a presidência em 2023, após o afastamento de Roberto Freire.

Quando Freire voltou ao cargo amparado por decisões da Justiça do Distrito Federal, uma ala do partido contestou seu retorno e defendeu que Comte continuasse à frente da legenda.

De volta à presidência, Freire deu andamento à convocação de um congresso para escolher o novo dirigente. Comte tentou impedir, mas o TSE negou o recurso. O congresso foi realizado em 4 de março e elegeu Alex Manente.

articles.title: Campanha Natal Solidário arrecada brinquedos para crianças em Varginha | G1
articles.standfirst: Iniciativa da EPTV e da ACIV vai até 19 de dezembro. Doações serão direcionadas para entidades.

articles.body:
EPTV e ACIV fazem campanha para arrecadar brinquedos para crianças no Natal em Varginha — Foto: Reprodução/TV Gazeta

A EPTV e a Associação Comercial, Industrial, Agropecuária e Serviços de Varginha (ACIV) estão realizando a campanha "Natal Solidário" de arrecadação de brinquedos para alegrar o Natal de crianças.

As doações seguem até 19 de dezembro. Serão recebidos brinquedos novos ou em bom estado.

Para participar, basta ir até o ponto de coleta, que fica na sede da ACIV, na Rua Presidente Antônio Carlos, nº 303, no Centro.

Os brinquedos arrecadados serão direcionados a entidades que atendem crianças.

A campanha também terá pontos de arrecadação em São Carlos, Araraquara, Ribeirão Preto, Campinas e Americana, no estado de São Paulo.

“É papel de uma emissora com a capilaridade da EPTV promover ações em parceria com a sociedade civil com o propósito de transformar o dia a dia de milhares de crianças. Uma das premissas do Grupo EP é justamente fortalecer os laços com a comunidade e, sobretudo, estreitar ainda mais essa relação por meio de campanhas como esta”, afirma o diretor Institucional da EPTV, Cleber Mata.

articles.title: Alexandre de Moraes se declara suspeito em ação sobre indenizações | G1
articles.standfirst: Ministro alegou questão de foro íntimo. Foi no âmbito dessa ação que o ministro Flávio Dino autorizou a abertura de uma investigação da PF para apurar suspeitas de interferência estrangeira nas eleições deste ano.
articles.summary: Alexandre de Moraes se declara suspeito em ação sobre indenizações no exterior que gerou investigação da PF sobre interferência estrangeira nas eleições brasileiras.
articles.body:
O ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ), se declarou suspeito para julgar uma ação na Corte que discute a possibilidade de municípios brasileiros ajuizarem ações judiciais no exterior para cobrar indenizações por danos causados em território nacional.

A ação sobre indenizações envolvendo mineradoras tramita no Supremo desde 2024. A última determinação no caso foi justamente a abertura do inquérito no fim de outubro (entenda mais abaixo).

O Supremo informou apenas que a decisão do ministro foi tomada por foro íntimo , como registrado no despacho. O Código de Processo Civil prevê que o juiz pode se declarar suspeito sem precisar expor suas razões.

🔎Na decisão, Dino cita notícias de possível financiamento estrangeiro de campanha e menciona a Rockbridge Network, que teria participado de negociações para apoiar Flávio Bolsonaro (PL).

Após a abertura do inquérito pela PF, a investigação foi desmembrada do processo original e passou a tramitar em procedimento separado, sob sigilo.

Alexandre de Moraes em sessão plenária do STF — Foto: Antonio Augusto/STF

O caso que Moraes se declarou suspeito para julgar trata-se de uma ação apresentada pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração (Ibram) ao Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), em junho de 2024. O processo é relatado pelo ministro Flávio Dino.

No processo, o Ibram questiona a atuação de municípios brasileiros que contrataram escritórios de advocacia estrangeiros para processar empresas no exterior.

Entre os casos envolvidos estão ações relacionadas aos desastres ambientais de Mariana e Brumadinho, em Minas Gerais.

O instituto argumentou que os municípios não poderiam atuar dessa forma sem observar as regras constitucionais sobre soberania nacional e competências da União. Também questionou os contratos firmados com escritórios estrangeiros, especialmente aqueles que previam pagamento de honorários condicionado ao resultado das ações.

Em novembro de 2024, Moraes chegou a votar na ação sobre mineração no plenário virtual do Supremo.

Na época, o ministro acompanhou o voto do relator, Flávio Dino, para determinar que municípios afetados pelo rompimento da barragem de Fundão, em Mariana (MG), apresentem os contratos eventualmente celebrados com escritórios de advocacia para atuarem em outros países e para que se abstenham de pagar honorários relativos às ações judiciais perante tribunais estrangeiros.

Em outubro de 2026, o PT apresentou, dentro do processo, um pedido para que fossem apurados indícios de possível interferência estrangeira nas eleições brasileiras.

Flávio Dino considerou que os elementos apresentados justificavam uma investigação da Polícia Federal. Determinou que a PF apurasse, entre outros pontos, possíveis financiamentos estrangeiros de campanhas, a atuação de redes políticas internacionais e eventuais manipulações de algoritmos de plataformas digitais.

A investigação foi determinada no âmbito da ação, mas deveria tramitar separadamente, sob sigilo e supervisão do STF.

articles.title: Deputy FBI director to retire in December, Washington Post reports
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Christopher Raia, the FBI's deputy director, intends to retire in December, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing thr...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 23 (Reuters) - Christopher Raia, the FBI's deputy director, intends to retire in ‌December, the Washington Post reported on ‌Monday, citing three people familiar with the matter, marking ​the latest departure from the bureau during the Trump administration.

The FBI and the US Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a ‌request for comment.

Raia, ⁠a longtime FBI career official, was tapped in January to replace right-wing ⁠podcaster and former Secret Service agent Dan Bongino, who was regarded as unconventional pick for ​the role.

Before ​this role, Raia was ​assistant director in ‌charge of the New York Field Office and has been with the FBI since 2003, previously serving as a top counterterrorism official.

Major personnel changes have taken place at the FBI during ‌Trump's second term in ​which political experts have raised ​concerns over ​the president's use of federal probes ‌to go after political opponents ​and critics.

The ​Trump administration has seen some personnel changes across agencies since Republicans suffered defeats in ​the US ‌midterm elections in November.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh ​in Washington; Editing by Ryan Patrick ​Jones and Caitlin Webbber)

articles.title: Judge unseals documents related to search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home
articles.summary: Some of the unsealed court filings make clear the Trump administration believes violations of the law took place as far back as 1980.
articles.body: A federal judge unsealed more than 160 pages’ worth of court documents Monday night pertaining to the warrant authorizing a federal search of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Washington, D.C. Chief U.S. District Judge James E. Boasberg ruled that some of the documents could be released with redactions after a coalition of news publications, including NBCUniversal News Group, sought access to the sealed records. The released documents do not include the search warrant. Boasberg agreed with the Justice Department in its efforts to keep the majority of the records sealed, but said a back-and-forth regarding the protection of Omar’s “speech or debate” rights — a clause that shields lawmakers from criminal and civil liability tied to legislative acts — should be made public. About half of the pages are mostly or entirely redacted from public view, but what is clear from the unredacted portions is the length to which a magistrate judge worked to ensure the Trump administration was following proper procedures for executing a search warrant on a member of Congress. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh asked the Justice Department several times for briefings explaining its theory of probable cause, and the DOJ said the process included “several rounds” of affidavit revisions. Sharbaugh ultimately found that the speech or debate clause was at least in part relevant, because it was a search of Omar’s home. As a result, “special search procedures” were carried out at Omar’s home, according to the unsealed documents. The list of property the government planned to seize from Omar’s home is largely redacted — and the list of property they took is entirely redacted — but unredacted documents indicate it included “All records and information that constitute fruits, contraband, evidence, and instrumentalities of violations of (REDACTED).” The government also planned to seize papers, records, photographs, documents, thumb drives, external hard drives, computers, or other electronic media devices holding any of the above records or documents, along with cellphones and any digital device owned, used or controlled by Omar that could have contained evidence of wrongdoing. Omar previously said that federal agents took 17 items from her home, including old phones which she said belonged to her and one of her daughters. The filings unsealed Monday also make clear the length of time the government believed violations of the law took place — between 1980 to the present. Omar’s congressional bio page says she was born in October 1982. “The United States believes ILHAN has committed (REDACTED) crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” another filing submitted to the court by Associate Deputy Attorney General Alessandra Serano reads. “Nothing in the search warrant affidavit, briefing, or oral argument indicates that the United States’s case has anything to do with ILHAN’s professional life.” Omar’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment regarding the released documents. The congresswoman’s home was searched in October, within weeks of the midterm elections, an unusual move to take against a sitting lawmaker seeking re-election. The DOJ has kept the charges against the Minnesota Democrat under wraps, but people familiar with the investigation previously told NBC News that they revolve around potential immigration-related crimes. Omar is a naturalized citizen, who immigrated to the U.S. from Somalia when she was a child. Omar has called the search “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” President Donald Trump has repeatedly taken political shots at Omar, and at Somalis more generally. When speaking about the congresswoman at his rallies, crowds of Trump’s supporters have sometimes erupted into chants of “lock her up.” The president has denied any involvement with the search of Omar’s house.

articles.summary: Local law enforcement is appealing for tips after a weekend camping trip along the Blackwater River ended in tragedy for a Florida official's family.
articles.body: A newly elected Florida politician is mourning the death of his son after the young man was fatally shot inside his tent during a weekend camping trip, his father confirmed Monday. Joe Vinson, who made history earlier this year as the first non-party-affiliated county commissioner elected in Escambia County, announced the tragedy on Instagram, revealing that his son, Carey Washington Vinson, was killed while camping with friends near the Blackwater River in the Florida Panhandle. RUSH HOUR ROAD RAGE SUSPECT’S BAIL REVOKED AS SLAIN UTILITY WORKER’S SUPPORTERS SHOUT AT ACCUSED MURDERER Carey, 19, and his friends had been camping on sandbars along the river since Friday, Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told People magazine. articles.title: White House sends Congress ‘anomalies’ request to keep federal agencies funded
articles.summary: The White House is asking Congress to include billions of dollars in additional funding in a stopgap spending bill to fund federal agencies that lawmakers are expected to take up next month. The 12-page “anomalies” request sent Monday, reported by Politico, outlines a series of exceptions to current spending levels that would allow the Trump…
articles.body:
The White House is asking Congress to include billions of dollars in additional funding in a stopgap spending bill to fund federal agencies that lawmakers are expected to take up next month.

The 12-page “ anomalies ” request sent Monday, reported by Politico, outlines a series of exceptions to current spending levels that would allow the Trump administration to advance some of its biggest policy priorities even if Congress fails to reach an agreement on full-year government funding.

Among the administration’s requests is a $5 billion annualized funding rate for the Golden Dome, President Trump’s ambitious plan to build a missile defense shield over the U.S. The White House warned that without the provision, the program would be “unable to continue production” that began with funding from the “One Big Beautiful Bill” Act.

The White House is also seeking roughly $21.3 billion in annualized funding increases for the Navy’s submarine programs, as well as authority to begin purchasing materials to build the first “Trump-class” battleship.

Lawmakers are set to face a Dec. 11 deadline to avert a government shutdown when they return to D.C. next week. With little progress toward a bipartisan spending agreement, Congress will likely pursue another continuing resolution before Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

The document indicates that additional Pentagon funding requests are forthcoming as the Trump administration’s push for a $1.5 trillion defense budget stalls in Congress.

Beyond military spending, the White House is seeking billions to fund NASA’s Artemis program to return American astronauts to the moon, as well as additional funding for wildfire suppression to address potential shortfalls.

There is also a request for a $70 million annualized increase for infectious disease surveillance programs at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The administration warned that federal funding allocated during the COVID-19 pandemic will run out by the beginning of January.

The spending negotiations also present an opportunity for the administration to revisit a contentious provision restricting the sale of hemp-derived products.

Congress in September temporarily delayed a ban on intoxicating hemp products that was set to take effect last month. With that reprieve set to expire Dec. 11, the White House is asking lawmakers to revise federal law to preserve access to nonintoxicating CBD products while maintaining restrictions on products that pose health risks and preventing their sale to children.

articles.title: Massachusetts sues Trump admin to stop ICE's courthouse arrests: 'Unnecessary fear'
articles.summary: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration over ICE's courthouse arrests without judicial warrants, saying they violate a new state law.
articles.body: Massachusetts officials sued the Trump administration on Monday to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from carrying out civil arrests in the state's courthouses, arguing that such arrests without judicial warrants are illegal under state law. The lawsuit filed by Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell challenges a 2025 ICE directive that authorizes agents to conduct civil arrests in or near state courthouses without judicial warrants, which she says violates the PROTECT Act, a new state law passed ​by the Democratic-led legislature that prohibits civil immigration arrests in state courthouses without judicial warrants. The courthouse protections took effect Nov. 3. Campbell said the ICE directive interferes with the state's authority to operate its judicial system, disrupts court proceedings, undermines constitutional principles and public safety and spreads fear, chaos and confusion. "The Massachusetts PROTECT Act makes it illegal for ICE to conduct civil arrests in our courthouses without a judicial warrant. ICE’s intentional violation of state law has created unnecessary fear, made it more difficult to operate our courts and hold defendants accountable," Campbell said in a statement. DOJ SUES TO STOP OHIO COURT BLOCKING COURTHOUSE ARRESTS "ICE is misleading the public by suggesting that these arrests make us safer when, in fact, ICE's actions are preventing criminal cases from moving forward, denying a victim’s ability to obtain accountability, violating a defendant’s due process, and leaving open the possibility that someone facing serious criminal charges could ultimately be released from ICE custody without their criminal case ever being resolved," she continued. The attorney general said more than 1,110 people have been arrested at her state's courthouses since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, including more than 600 people in 2025 and more than 500 during the first 10 months of 2026. Campbell said ICE has ignored the new state law and arrested at least 38 people in Massachusetts courthouses without judicial warrants in the two and a half weeks since the courthouse protections went into effect. "I, along with our district attorneys, share the goal of holding defendants accountable for crimes, yet ICE’s unlawful tactics to arrest someone for a civil immigration violation is not the same as holding them accountable for a crime," Campbell said. FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS Campbell said that ICE's courthouse arrests have continued in Massachusetts despite a federal ruling handed down in June by U.S. District Judge P. Casey Pitts in California that vacated the Trump administration's courthouse arrest policy ​in a separate class action lawsuit. In Monday's lawsuit, Campbell argues the ICE policy violates the Administrative Procedure Act since it was adopted without taking into account the impact it would have on states and because the Immigration and Nationality Act does not explicitly authorize courthouse arrests. The lawsuit also alleges that the ⁠policy violates the U.S. Constitution's Tenth Amendment, which protects states' rights to maintain authority over their own judicial systems. "The Trump Administration’s ICE arrests at Massachusetts courthouses are interfering with our justice system and undermining public safety. When people are afraid to go to court, victims are less likely to report crimes, survivors are less likely to seek protection, and our communities are less safe," Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said in a statement. "We expect ICE and all federal agents to follow Massachusetts law." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. In a statement to Reuters, a DHS spokesperson argued that making immigration arrests at courthouses "conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already ​know where a target will ​be," adding that "the ability of law enforcement ⁠to make arrests of criminal illegal aliens in courthouses is common sense." A similar lawsuit against ICE arrests at state courthouses was filed in October by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

articles.summary: El presidente del PSOE responde a las manifestaciones del político catalán
articles.body: La política mezclada con el deporte. El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha salido al paso de las declaraciones del alcalde de Badalona, Xavier García Albiol, después de que este mostrara en una entrevista concedida a Sport su decisión de no ponerse la camiseta de la selección de Lamien Yamal. En ella señalaba el dirigente catalán que era un confeso espanyolista cuando le cuestionaron si se pondría esa camiseta con el dorsal de Lamine aseguró: "No, es que a mí Yamal me cae un poco mal. Lo digo con sinceridad". Y añadía sus razones: "Pues porque... Lo he dicho un poco, ¿eh? Porque... No lo sé, no lo sé. Sí que pienso que por su forma un poco de ser, ¿no? Sí que creo que ha madurado bastante en los últimos años o algo así, pero es que al principio era muy tonto, ¿eh? O sea, en el sentido de comportamiento, no de fútbol, que creo que es un fuera de serie". Ahora bien, quiso añadir que "también creo que ha madurado y está siendo más serio que al principio. Era un poco...". Eso sí, apostilló que se sentiría más cómodo luciendo la camiseta de cualquier otro jugador del Barcelona que estuviera en la selección a excepción de Joan García, que es un ex del Espanyol. Esas palabras han hecho mella política y ha sido Pedro Sánchez el que ha saltado al respecto. El jefe del Ejecutivo ha añadido un vídeo en su red social 'X' poniéndose la camiseta de Lamine Yamal y ha dejado un mensaje al respecto incluyendo la entrevista realizada en Mundo deportivo. "Yo me pondría la camiseta de cualquier jugador o jugadora de la Selección Española de Fútbol. Porque eso es España, un país plural y diverso. Os dejo, para cerrar el día, mi entrevista en Mundo Deportivo", dejaba constancia.

articles.title: Raskin probes government benefits to companies affiliated with Donald Trump Jr. firm
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, is expanding his probe into Donald Trump Jr. and an investment firm he partnered with shortly after his father was reelected. The lawmaker sent letters to the four partners of 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm that previously declined to provide requested materials…
articles.body:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (Md.), the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, is expanding his probe into Donald Trump Jr. and an investment firm he partnered with shortly after his father was reelected.

The lawmaker sent letters to the four partners of 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm that previously declined to provide requested materials to Raskin and accused him of a “spaghetti-against-the-wall approach.”

Raskin’s letters were sent to three companies, including well known entities like Polymarket and Juul, he argues have been the “beneficiary of 1789 Capital’s serendipitous timing,” including favorable actions from government regulators. A fourth letter was sent to Hadrian, which was awarded government contracts after the venture capital firm’s investment.

“1789 Capital has become remarkably adept at ‘timing’ its investments in companies shortly before they benefited from lucrative federal contracts and favorable regulatory actions, which are dispensed through the Trump Administration’s self-described ‘unitary executive’ chain of command,” Raskin wrote in a letter to Polymarket, a betting site.

That company, Raskin said, has since faced investigation over whether it was in violation of a 2022 Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) settlement prohibiting it from taking wagers in the U.S. That investigation was abandoned under the Trump administration, which later signed off on its acquisition of a derivatives exchange company, allowing it to enter the U.S. market.

“1789 Capital’s striking success in predicting both the imminent award of government contracts and the release of favorable regulatory actions to its portfolio or affiliated companies suggests that either (1) Donald Trump Jr. suddenly acquired and brought to 1789 Capital magical new clairvoyant powers that catapulted him to the position of greatest investor of all time,” Raskin wrote.

“Or (2) we are witnessing a brazen conspiracy to use the machinery of the executive branch of government under the control of President Trump to rig both public policy and the markets in order to enrich the First Family beyond the wildest dreams of any other presidential family, not to mention the vast majority of Americans.”

The letter to Haridan focuses on a Navy contract to make submarine parts and an Army contract to build a facility to manufacture weapons systems, despite being what Raskin called a “nascent manufacturing company with…no history of fulfilling government contracts.”

The contracts came after the company made several large campaign donations to Trump-aligned political action committees.

“Your investment in the Trump family has paid handsome dividends,” the lawmaker wrote.

“Hadrian’s valuation quintupled from $1.6 billion to nearly $8 billion following the announcements, inescapably generating immense returns for yourself and 1789 Capital.”

The letter to Hadiran comes after President Trump late Friday signed an executive order seeking to limit government contractors from complying with congressional inquiries.

1789 Capital’s attorneys said Raskin had launched a baseless inquiry into the company.

“We responded to Congressman Raskin back in September pointing out in detail the many flaws in his understanding of how 1789 has operated and a number of basic factual errors. He never bothered to reply. Facts are facts and Congressman Raskin has them wrong here but persists in his tall tales against 1789,” attorney Bill Burck said in a statement.

“These are personal attacks untethered to actual evidence.”

Other actions, Raskin argued, benefited partners of 1789 Capital.

That includes GrabAGun, which he argues could benefit from a Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) rule that would make it easier to ship guns to people’s homes.

“In a May 13, 2026, press release, GrabAGun bragged that it was ‘uniquely positioned to capitalize on this potential opportunity,’” Raskin wrote.

GrabAGun denied that its connections to Donald Trump Jr. had any bearing on the outcome of the ATF rule.

“Congressman Raskin’s letter is a political document, and its allegations are baseless. ATF’s review of its regulations was well known across the firearms industry, and the agency published numerous proposed rules for public comment. GrabAGun’s only input came through public comments on several of those proposals,” the company said in a statement.

“We support ATF’s goal of modernizing outdated rules and focusing enforcement on violent crime.”

Another letter sent to Juul said that the partner of 1789 Capital benefited when “suddenly, FDA’s concerns about kids getting hooked on flavored e-cigarettes began to dissipate.”

Raskin noted that the FDA was also taking action to approve more types of flavored e-cigarettes.

“A few short months later, FDA approved the marketing of three new ‘JUUL2’ e-cigarette products, at which time, you announced Juul would pursue a ‘robust series of FDA filings’ for ‘a portfolio of flavors—beyond tobacco and menthol.’”

Hadrian and Polymarket did not immediately respond to request for comment.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE: Group forms to draft Rand Paul to run for president in 2028
articles.summary: A new group has formed to draft Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) to run for president in 2028, something that Paul says he will consider over the next several months. Draft Rand, which describes itself as an independent grassroots movement, has launched a new website, DraftRand.com, to persuade Paul, who ran for president in 2016, to…
articles.body:
A new group has formed to draft Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) to run for president in 2028, something that Paul says he will consider over the next several months.

Draft Rand, which describes itself as an independent grassroots movement, has launched a new website, DraftRand.com, to persuade Paul, who ran for president in 2016, to jump into the race.

Paul told The Hill he sees a lane for someone to run for the White House as a traditional fiscal conservative who would favor rolling back President Trump’s tariffs and ending the prolonged military conflict with Iran, which has caused gas and diesel prices to soar.

“I think there needs to be a candidate who’s pro-international trade and the benefits that come with it, against deficits, against the trade war and the Iran war, and I don’t think there are that many people out there really,” Paul said.

“Most of the people from here that might want to run have already voted to raise the debt ceiling, they all voted for the trade war, they all voted for the Iran war. I think there might be a lane, but I haven’t made a decision,” he said.

Paul last year voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which raised the federal debt limit by $5 trillion from $36.1 trillion to $41.1 trillion.

Paul voted with Democrats and a few Republicans last year to unwind Trump’s global tariffs — joining Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine).

He also voted last year for a resolution to end tariffs on Brazil and Canada, two major U.S. trading partners.

And Paul has voted multiple times for Democratic-sponsored resolutions directing Trump to immediately end the Iran war unless he receives authorization to continue the conflict from Congress.

Conservatives who want to push the Republican Party to return to free-market values and strict adherence to the Constitution say that Paul would provide a promising alternative to the GOP’s current trajectory if he were to run for president.

“Senator Paul has said he will make his decision after the midterms, and we intend to make sure that when he does, he knows exactly how many Americans are ready to stand with him,” said Larry Ward, chair of Constitutional Rights PAC, a group helping to organize the Draft Rand effort.

“This effort is not about pointing fingers. It is about building something powerful. Fiscal conservatives, constitutional conservatives, liberty voters and independents all agree that Washington spends too much, spies too much and too often forgets that our foreign policy should protect the interests of the American people,” he said.

The effort to prod Paul to run for higher office will tout his efforts to balance the budget, scrutinize the COVID-19 policies promulgated under former chief medical adviser Anthony Fauci and end foreign wars.

Brian Darling, a GOP strategist who previously served as senior communications director and counsel to Paul, said the Kentucky lawmaker is able to withstand pressure and pushback from colleagues as he pursues his policy goals.

“He fought to balance the budget when it was unpopular in his own party. He fought for the Fourth Amendment when the surveillance establishment insisted it could not be done. He chased answers on COVID when the rest of Washington wanted to move on,” he said.

“That record is exactly why the coalition that came together around the liberty movement can come together again, and why it can win,” he argued.

Paul’s willingness to buck GOP leaders has drawn criticism from fellow Republicans in Washington.

Trump slammed Paul in June of last year for opposing his signature domestic legislative effort, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

“Rand votes NO on everything, but never has any practical or constructive ideas. His ideas are actually crazy (losers!). The people of Kentucky can’t stand him. This is a BIG GROWTH BILL!” Trump posted on Truth Social at the time.

Paul’s allies, however, think that voters may be more open to Paul’s call to return to conservative free-market and constitutional values after they sent the president a stinging rebuke in the midterm election, which gave Democrats big new majorities in the Senate and House.

“Sen. Paul has a unique perspective within the Republican Party when it comes to restrained foreign policy, not a fan of tariffs and somebody who wants to take a hard look at the national debt and how to tackle it,” Darling said.

Other Republicans who have been discussed as potential White House candidates in 2028 include Vice President Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, former Virginia Gov. Glenn Youngkin and Sen. Tom Cotton (Ark.).

articles.title: A round of pirate golf at East Potomac
articles.summary: There is something that, since I was a boy, I’ve thought of as “Florida weather.” It rolls into the mid-Atlantic most Novembers. It’s unseasonably warm and the air is pregnant with the storms that will follow. After a winter trip to Miami when I was 6 or 7 years old, those balmy days in the…
articles.body:
There is something that, since I was a boy, I’ve thought of as “Florida weather.” It rolls into the mid-Atlantic most Novembers. It’s unseasonably warm and the air is pregnant with the storms that will follow.

After a winter trip to Miami when I was 6 or 7 years old, those balmy days in the wrong place on the calendar back home became fused with Florida in my mind. It’s like if someone of a certain age hears the term “Pizza Hut cup,” it doesn’t matter what Pizza Hut is actually slinging its Pepsi in these days, their mind will immediately conjure a short, stout tumbler of pebbled red plastic. If it’s the late fall and we have a couple of humid days with low, cottony clouds and it’s over 60 degrees, it’s always Florida weather to me.

It may come as early as Halloween or as late as Thanksgiving, but it is always the heavy, warm air that follows the crisp afternoons of autumn and precedes the arrival of real winter. It is like hitting the thermocline in the descent into those weeks when the trees are bare, the ground is hard and some mornings start to smell like snow.

We’ve had a big dose of Florida weather in Washington this year. The leaves are mostly down, but when that slanty afternoon sun starts burning through the clouds there is something very lovely in the air, but also something extremely unsettled — something charged.

It was a day just like that my youngest manchild and I crossed into the unknown at East Potomac Park out on Hains Point, a little spit of land that sticks out into the river in Southeast D.C. It juts down from where the National Mall meets the river at the Jefferson Memorial and kind of dangles out there across from Reagan National, where we watched regional jets as skinny as toothpicks and long-haul widebodies take turns chewing through the heavy air to get altitude over the capital city.

It’s a space in-between on a day between seasons, made all the more uncertain by the fact that what we were there to do was, while not exactly illegal, was most certainly unsanctioned.

President Trump has been on a bombing campaign of sorts against the city’s western riverfront. You probably heard about the Kennedy Center, which sits abandoned and decaying just south of Georgetown. Since the courts won’t allow it to be renamed to include Trump’s name, he has decided to let it fall apart. When I take the high, banked turn onto Interstate 66 past the building several times each week, I go past the tarp placed over the current and former presidents’ names, it reminds me of someone pulling a sheet over a dead body’s face.

Just to the south of that is the intended site of the president’s triumphal arch, which would tower 150 feet over the nearby Lincoln Memorial and might or might not, depending on that day’s court filings, be a military installation for snipers and drones. Right now it’s just a bunch of equipment ringed by traffic barrels and orange plastic fencing on the Virginia side of the Memorial Bridge. The administration wants to be ready to start piling up stones if ever an injunction lapses. A project once begun is hard to stop, so they don’t want to miss a chance.

But Hains Point has been the most recent theater of war for the battle between Trump and the District of Columbia.

East Potomac Golf Course began its life as a civil engineering project. In the late nineteenth century, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers dragged up millions of cubic yards of mud while dredging the river channels, piling the whole mess into a flat, wind-whipped finger of earth. Then in 1897, Congress declared it a public park to be preserved “forever.” Problem was, there wasn’t much to do with what had only recently been a pile of silt.

But golf, which at the turn of the century was opening up to more and more middle-class Americans, might work. Hains Point, if you squint, does seem to have a little of the Scottish Links to it. In 1911, park officials enlisted Walter J. Travis, three-time U.S. Amateur champion turned course designer, to bring the spirit of St. Andrews to the Potomac. Delayed by World War I, the initial nine holes finally opened in 1920. Another nine came online in 1923, and a third two years later.

Trump has a plan to replace the three municipal courses with one big 18-hole track that can host professional tournaments and be a showpiece for the government. To do so, he has to push out the National Links Trust, the non-profit that took over operation of the courses as part of a deal with the Park Service in Trump’s first term. And like the efforts up the river, Trump’s big plans for East Potomac have ended up snarled in endless litigation.

So, the courses are in limbo. Trump was able to force the National Links Trust out and rip out a bunch of trees, but has been stopped from ripping the whole thing up — for now. So, like the French leaving Indochina, the Park Service pulled out everything that wasn’t bolted down — every tiny golf pencil, every cup and flagstick. But you can’t pack up a 220-acre golf course complex.

What happened next was a kind of miracle of spontaneous order. The devoted golfers of East Potomac showed up anyway, some with makeshift flags, others with leafblowers brought from home and they just played. There are no starters on loudspeakers, no marshals policing pace of play, no clatter of balls in hoppers at the driving range. It’s just golf.

A perfect place to kick through some leaves and join the quiet, smiling parade of golfers out in the glow of some fine Florida weather: Dads pushing sleeping infants in strollers, old timers walking instead of riding for a change, first-timers out to see what all the fuss was about. Nor did it hurt that there wasn’t anyone there to collect the greens fees…

Who knows what comes next for East Potomac or Washington or this administration, but there on a balmy November afternoon we saw a great reminder that Americans can figure most of the big questions out for ourselves.

articles.title: Shutdown odds rise as senators scramble for fragile deal on Iran
articles.summary: Senate negotiators are trying to thread the needle and find a deal to avoid a government shutdown before Christmas, but progress has been slowed by a Senate Democratic leadership fight. The key issue is the Iran war, which was a major factor in the sweeping Democratic midterm election victories. Senate negotiators are sketching the outlines…
articles.body:
Senate negotiators are trying to thread the needle and find a deal to avoid a government shutdown before Christmas, but progress has been slowed by a Senate Democratic leadership fight.

The key issue is the Iran war, which was a major factor in the sweeping Democratic midterm election victories.

Senate negotiators are sketching the outlines of a deal that would provide the Trump administration with critical funding to replenish weapons and munitions stockpiles that have been depleted by the Iran war, but that would purport to stop funding the conflict itself.

The question is whether that deal can be accepted by progressive Democrats who have called for an immediate end to the war, or by President Trump, as his administration would get far less money than it sought.

And then there’s the complication of the Senate leadership fight pitting progressive Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) against Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.).

That battle is putting pressure on Schumer to keep his distance from the funding talks, since it could cost him support within his own conference.

Senators in both parties say they desperately want to avoid another shutdown, but party strategists say the odds of one increase each day Congress lurches closer to the Dec. 11 deadline.

“A government shutdown is a greater probability every day that goes by that Republicans and Democrats aren’t talking to each other,” said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and former Senate leadership aide.

“The postelection lame duck has a recipe for a long, drawn-out process of a government shutdown,” he said. “You have Democrats who feel emboldened and a president who’s ready for a fight by hiring Stephen Miller as his chief of staff.”

Republicans say senior members of the Senate and House Appropriations committees are trying to lay the groundwork for a deal but warn that the talks won’t make substantial progress until Schumer, whose internal Senate leadership election is Dec. 1, gets involved directly.

“We’re not sure what’s going to come together,” said a Republican senator, who added that senators have a House-passed bill that they could bring to the floor quickly to fund the government.

The GOP source cautioned that Democratic colleagues don’t want to vote for any measure that could be criticized by progressive activists as funding the Iran war.

“We want military funding. The Dems have things they want, which is fine. The other thing is for [Democrats] to feel like the money isn’t going to the conflict in Iran. That’s one of the tricky parts,” the senator said.

Republican leaders believe Trump can only bring the conflict to a swift conclusion if the Pentagon is fully funded and he’s negotiating with Iran from a position of strength.

“We believe that you only end the conflict in Iran from a position of strength. You can’t limit our ability to be in a strong position, but [Democrats] want to know the money is going to munitions and Ukraine” and not to prolong the war.

Senate GOP sources say Schumer hasn’t played a significant role in the talks while defending against Van Hollen’s challenge from the left.

“We would like to get into the conversation about funding the government and whatever else comes with that as soon as possible,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), who says he is “pretty involved” in the talks, told reporters before the weeklong Thanksgiving recess. “I think there are some good conversations happening. No deals yet.”

Thune is not trying to pick off a group of eight to 10 Democrats to get a funding measure through the Senate — which is what he did in November 2025 to end a record-setting, 43-day shutdown.

Republicans familiar with the talks say Democrats are expressing openness to a funding deal that would direct any increases in defense funding to replenishing stockpiles or ramping up U.S. defense capabilities in space instead of to the conflict with Iran.

Senate Armed Services Committee Chair Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) said Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.), the ranking member on his panel, appears open to such a deal.

“I just talked to the once and future chairman of the Armed Services Committee. … He’s trying to frame a solution,” he said.

Democrats say that any funding to maintain the naval blockade of Iranian ports or to conduct other activities that could be defined as “acts of war” toward Iran cannot come out of new money appropriated in a December funding deal.

Given the dwindling number of legislative days left in the year, senators are looking at a potential deal that would fund the government through mid-April and include the annual defense authorization bill, disaster relief and emergency assistance for farmers.

A Democratic senator who requested anonymity to discuss the talks said the Pentagon has enough unspent funding to continue military operations against Iran even if Congress adds language to a short-term funding bill that prohibits new funding of the war.

“The Department of Defense has a gazillion dollars that they move around all the time kind of with impunity,” said the senator. “It’s not as if there’s some magic vote we can force that’s going to cause them to not do that. I also think some of my caucus members are legitimately concerned about the munition shortage.”

The Democratic lawmaker said the Pentagon’s budget for 2026 was approved before Trump ordered strikes against Iran at the end of February, which could allow Democrats to argue that voting for a continuation of current funding levels would not be the same as voting to prolong the war.

Even so, Democratic senators are wary not to support any funding deal that could be attacked by progressive colleagues and activists as a vote to continue the war.

Van Hollen issued a joint statement with several colleagues, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), declaring that any short-term funding package “must include language that restricts the Trump administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

Trump has demanded that Thune circumvent Democratic opposition and immediately move a budget resolution to provide an additional $350 billion to the Pentagon. GOP sources, however, say there aren’t enough Senate Republican votes to do that — at least not now.

If the bipartisan negotiations fail, then GOP senators will look to use a budget reconciliation package to circumvent Democratic opposition and fund the Pentagon, but that time-consuming process would take weeks.

There is hardly enough time to get a reconciliation bill passed by Dec. 11, even if Republicans manage to muster 50 votes to pass both a budget resolution and then a follow-up reconciliation package.

It would require Senate and House Republicans to first pass the same budget resolution simply to unlock the budget reconciliation process.

Such a resolution would instruct the committees of jurisdiction to craft a reconciliation package, which then would be subject to lengthy debate and an unlimited series of amendment votes before final passage.

Each measure would consume several days of Senate floor time.

Senate GOP aides say they doubt whether Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will be able to enforce full Republican attendance in the House to ensure the passage of a budget resolution or reconciliation bill.

Senior Republican senators such as Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (Maine) and Sen. Mitch McConnell (Ky.), chair of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, are telling colleagues they want to fund the Pentagon through the regular appropriations process instead of using a budget reconciliation bill.

articles.title: What the US gets from Israel alliance as support for aid to the Jewish State erodes on left and right: report
articles.summary: A new report calls Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East, citing missile-defense co-production across 34 states as a key return.
articles.body: The U.S.-Israel alliance was tested when Washington and Jerusalem found common cause against Iran — and when defending Israel drew heavily on American weapons stocks. Meanwhile, that ongoing conflict has now sharpened a question for Washington: what does the alliance deliver, and what does it demand in return? A new report from Advancing American Freedom (AAF) and the Zionist Organization of America (ZOA) argues that Israel’s military reach and regional role make the alliance a strategic asset for Washington. Its authors call Israel "the largest U.S. aircraft carrier" in the Middle East. But this is in direct opposition of critics who say that the alliance costs the U.S. a lot and delivers very little in return. The report, dated Oct. 26, 2026, arrives as public support for Israel continues to fall across the political spectrum — even among Republicans and MAGA supporters. FROM INTELLIGENCE SHARING TO MISSILE DEFENSE, HOW ISRAEL'S PARTNERSHIP PROTECTS AMERICAN SECURITY President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed ending direct U.S. military aid, but the U.S. leader has also called Israel "a great ally, much more reliable than most" and said Washington would help if Israel needed it. The report specifically points to intelligence sharing, joint weapons development and military cooperation as returns on what the U.S. gets for providing support to Israel. One of the clearest examples is missile defense. The U.S. and Israel develop systems including David’s Sling and Arrow, while American companies manufacture components for several programs. More than 100 companies across 34 states participate in missile-defense co-production, according to the Congressional Research Service. In August, a Raytheon-Rafael facility in Arkansas delivered the first Iron Dome Tamir interceptor built entirely in the U.S. Those programs support U.S. manufacturers and give the Pentagon a role in developing missile-defense systems. During the Iran conflict, however, U.S. forces also expended large numbers of interceptors — costly weapons that can take years to replace. US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES In September, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) estimated that the U.S. had probably used between half and two-thirds of its combined inventory of Patriot, THAAD, SM-3 and SM-6 interceptors since June 2025. The estimate includes weapons used during the earlier 12-day war with Iran and is based on publicly reported expenditures compared with the number of those interceptors the War Department has purchased. CBO said rebuilding stocks could take at least five years, even if production increased. Intelligence sharing is another return cited by supporters of the alliance. Former CIA Director John Brennan said Israeli intelligence was among the "thousands of bits" considered during the years-long effort to find Usama bin Laden. He did not specify what Israel provided or how much it contributed to the operation. A more recent exchange shows how Israeli reporting can prompt U.S. action even when its accuracy is uncertain. Israeli officials warned the U.S. of a possible Iranian plot to kill Trump during a trip to Turkey. The Secret Service took precautions, including moving him to another aircraft. U.S. intelligence agencies could not independently verify the threat, however, and the CIA assessed some of the Israeli reporting with "low confidence," according to Reuters and The Washington Post. NETANYAHU REVEALS HE WANTS AMERICAN FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR ISRAEL TO 'DRAW DOWN TO ZERO' The financial relationship has also become part of the debate. Under the current agreement, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing and $500 million for joint missile-defense programs. Most of the military aid pays for weapons and services from U.S. contractors, according to CRS. Israel’s ability to spend a portion of the funding on domestic purchases is scheduled to phase out by 2028. The report's authors call the $3.8 billion in annual U.S. military aid "one of the highest returns on investment of any U.S. foreign assistance." Trump has said he wants to end annual aid, while Netanyahu has also publicly called for phasing it out over time. U.S. and Israeli officials have been negotiating a new agreement that could wind down direct assistance while expanding joint defense projects and weapons production. The current agreement runs through 2028, Congress controls appropriations, and no successor deal has been reached. TRUMP WANTS LARGEST-EVER ISRAELI HEAVY BOMB TRANSFER — BUT PROPOSAL HAS CONGRESS PREPARING FOR $2.8B FIGHT The debate is also becoming more politically consequential as Americans question the relationship’s terms. A 2026 Chicago Council survey found that 56% favored reducing or ending U.S. military aid to Israel. Republicans remain more supportive than Democrats and independents, but the right is divided: Joe Kent blamed Israeli pressure for the Iran war, Rep. Thomas Massie has pushed to cut aid, and Vice President JD Vance has called for changing the relationship while continuing to describe Israel as a strategic ally. The two countries have cooperated against Iran and developed defenses against missile attacks, but their goals have not always matched during the war. A Stimson Center analysis says Israel sought to broaden the conflict beyond what Washington preferred. That does not establish that Israel drew the United States into a war it opposed. It does show how cooperation can leave Washington managing military costs even when its preferred limits differ from Israel’s. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The next agreement will help determine whether the alliance continues to rely on direct grants or shifts toward joint weapons development and production. Either way, the military and intelligence cooperation described in the report comes with commitments of U.S. money and weapons — and leaves Washington weighing those costs against the advantages it expects the alliance to deliver.

articles.title: Trump welcomes turkeys to the White House for Thanksgiving pardon as farmer dishes on prep for the big day
articles.summary: West Virginia farmer Scott Rightsell trained "Freedom" and "Feathers" for the White House turkey pardon, getting the 40-pound birds used to loud noises.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will participate in the annual Turkey Pardon on Tuesday, and the West Virginia turkey farmer responsible for raising this year's two birds helps walk Fox News Digital through the process from hatch to White House ahead of the light-hearted event. "We spent a little bit more one-on-one time with each of these birds to get them trained to loud noises, a lot of people present, flashing lights — just being handled — so when they get to the president, hopefully they'll act like they have some sense," Scott Rightsell told Fox News Digital about raising the birds for Tuesday's National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon. Rightsell, who owns and operates Deans Gap Farm in rural Fort Seybert, West Virginia, with his wife Becky, found out during the summer that he would raise the turkeys for the ceremony. He received the young turkeys in July — shortly after the celebration for America 250. A White House spokesperson tells Fox News Digital that Trump will deliver remarks about "how well our nation is doing" during the event just two days of the holiday. The turkeys were named Freedom and Feathers through a White House public opinion poll, beating out the options for Commander and Chief or Honey and Ham. TRUMP'S THANKSGIVING TURKEYS ARRIVE AT LUXURY DC HOTEL AS AMERICANS VOTE ON THEIR NAMES "We've had them from the middle of the July until now," said Rightsell. "The turkeys weigh probably 40 to 45 pounds right now." He added that besides the aforementioned training, the birds receive the same treatment as all the others that he raises on the farm, which he and his wife founded in 2015. "Being on national TV, that's a big deal," Rightsell said when asked what he was looking forward to most about his trip to the nation's capital this week. "I mean That's probably what we're looking forward to the most is being on national TV, actually meeting the president, which everybody does not get to do that. And getting to converse with him and the first lady, that's gonna be a real treat for us." Typically, the pardon event is held in the Rose Garden. However, Trump will host the pardoning on the new South Lawn helipad Tuesday afternoon. First lady Melania Trump, Vice President JD Vance and a litany of Cabinet secretaries, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Education Secretary Linda McMahon. Attorney General Todd Blanche will also attend. So will new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. "President Trump will participate in the time-honored American tradition and grant a Presidential Pardon to two turkeys, Freedom and Feathers. Guests will enjoy the 79th annual event on the new South Lawn Helipad for the first time this year, bringing a change of scenery to this enduring ceremony," White House spokesperson Allison Schuster told Fox News Digital. "Tune in to see President Trump spare these two birds from the Thanksgiving table and send them into retirement." The National Thanksgiving Turkey Pardon has been a tradition for 79 years, recurring annually since President Harry Truman occupied the White House, according to Christy Puffenbarger. Puffenbarger is this year's National Turkey Federation chairwoman, a position that rotates annually. She's the first woman to hold the role. Both turkeys receive a pardon, but which turkey participates in the ceremony depends on the American people, who vote for their preferred bird on the White House's website. INSIDE THE THANKSGIVING TURKEY HOTLINE THAT'S BEEN SAVING HOLIDAY DINNERS FOR 45 YEARS Neither bird will end up on the Thanksgiving dinner table. The turkey that doesn't receive a pardon remains behind the scenes at the White House, "for moral support," as Puffenbarger put it. If the chosen bird gets stage fright or cannot carry out the ceremonial duties, the second bird is on standby. "What I'm really looking forward to… is meeting the president and his wife and representing this industry," Puffenbarger told Fox News Digital. "[I] would like to thank the president for continuing this tradition. Because I do think it is a very nice event. It showcases not only our industry, but the tradition of turkey at Thanksgiving." Puffenbarger says the industry as a whole will provide 30 million pounds of turkey to Americans enjoying the Thanksgiving holiday this year. "And to be able to showcase it at a positive, fun event like that ... it'll be quite an honor for myself and my family," she said. After spending their first few months of life like any normal turkey, the royal treatment for Feathers and Freedom began on Thursday. They left for Washington, D.C., after a star-studded send-off from a local elementary school in Brandywine, West Virginia, where Becky Rightsell is also a teacher. Secretary Rollins attended the sendoff, as did West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey. "It’s so humbling for West Virginia to be named to have two of the turkeys that get pardoned. This is history in the making, only the second time that’s happened," Morrisey told WDTV during the ceremony. BROOKE ROLLINS, MONICA CROWLEY: AMERICA’S FAMILY FARMS HAVE KEPT US STRONG FOR 250 YEARS Sunday night, the birds arrived at the five-star Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington, D.C., where they received "presidential treatment," according to the Department of Agriculture (USDA), which posted photos of the turkeys sitting on the beds in a hotel room. A red carpet was rolled out as they strolled through the lobby of the hotel to much fanfare. Once in the room, the birds were greeted by a layer of crunchy fall leaves lining the floor. But the fun doesn't end after Tuesday's pardoning. Instead, the turkeys will be whisked away for their next adventure. "Immediately afterwards, another cool thing, these birds will get on an airplane and fly to beautiful College Station, Texas, where they will retire to live out the rest of their lives at Texas A&M University," Puffenbarger explained. Friday night, Texas A&M's football team is scheduled to host rival Texas, the fifth-ranked college football team in the country. Feathers and Freedom will be the guests of honor at the game. "I don't know how much they know about football, but I feel sure they will have a good time," Puffenbarger said.
