articles.title: US Army to proceed with Iowa detonation of degraded bomb materials: ‘A consensus decision’
articles.summary: The Army will detonate 68 barrels of crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown after a federal appeals court ruling.
articles.body: The U.S. Army will detonate 68 barrels of unstable, degraded bomb-making chemicals in Iowa on Wednesday morning after a federal appeals court rejected a legal challenge and allowed the controlled blast to move forward. In a statement late Monday, Army officials confirmed they are proceeding with destroying the crystallized lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown in coordination with state, local and federal authorities. "This is a consensus decision," Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle posted on social media. "Every expert agency agrees, and both Iowa’s current and incoming Governors say the call belongs to the experts." FEDERAL APPEALS COURT CLEARS ARMY TO DETONATE VOLATILE IOWA EXPLOSIVES AS DEM GOV-ELECT REFUSES TO SIGN OFF Hours earlier, a three-judge panel of the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals lifted a temporary pause and denied an emergency request from the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club to block the operation. The judges found that the Environmental Protection Agency built adequate safeguards into its emergency permit to limit lead dust dispersal. "Here we are faced with a situation in which the risk is between a controlled detonation and an unplanned explosion, not between the risk of a controlled detonation and no explosion at all," the court wrote. WATCH FOR A LOOK INSIDE THE IOWA AMMUNITION PLANT: The ruling followed a Truth Social post from President Donald Trump declaring he had ordered the military to hold off unless both the appeals court and Democratic Gov.-elect Rob Sand signed off. Trump warned he would hold Sand "responsible for any and all death or destruction" if the operation were blocked. Sand, who takes office in January, declined to approve or reject the blast on Monday evening. He posted on X that the Trump administration should make the call based on the experts it brought in months ago and urged federal officials to release their briefing details publicly. DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT Meanwhile, a flight carrying Army officials departed Joint Base Andrews for Iowa just before Trump's post went live. The operation has already been postponed three times amid public concern over toxic lead dust. Munitions specialists warned in court filings that dropping temperatures increase the risk that crystallized material inside the barrels could trigger an accidental, fatal explosion if left untreated. In a public advisory, the Army said Wednesday's blast will produce two rapid detonations, ground vibrations and a dust plume expected to linger for no more than an hour. Fox News Digital’s Alex Nitzberg and Sophia Compton, along with The Associated Press, contributed to this report.

articles.title: The security threat just might be coming from inside Trump’s White House
articles.summary: Silicon Valley awoke yesterday to some wild news: Just two weeks after Nvidia ousted its own founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Nvidia’s board ruled unanimously Monday morning to reinstate Huang. It happened just moments before trading began at 9 a.m., and by midday the company’s value had…
articles.body:
Silicon Valley awoke yesterday to some wild news: Just two weeks after Nvidia ousted its own founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Nvidia’s board ruled unanimously Monday morning to reinstate Huang. It happened just moments before trading began at 9 a.m., and by midday the company’s value had regained the more than $900 billion it lost upon Huang’s departure.

The decision, the board said, was made in consultation with the Trump administration, which we soon learned included President Trump himself, who had dialed into Nvidia’s board meeting to argue for Jensen’s return. According to White House communications director Steven Cheung, Trump “was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board.” A statement from Nvidia’s board, issued just after the news broke, confirmed that “in the process of reaching its decision, the board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

It was no secret that Trump strongly desired Huang’s return. He views Huang as indispensable to Nvidia, and Nvidia’s success as a company as indispensable to the thriving of the U.S. economy.

Huang’s reinstatement appears to reaffirm what we argued in these pages last week: The real crime was never the affair with a Chinese intelligence asset. It was the fact that the affair exposed a massive smuggling operation of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, in which Jensen Huang could not have been a mere dupe but had to be complicit — as was our own Commerce Department.

Huang’s reinstatement suggests that the Commerce Department was working at Trump’s behest.

The evidence surrounding Nvidia’s alleged knowledge of chip smuggling began to emerge right after Huang admitted to his affair with a woman named Alice Huang (no relation), who we now know was in touch with China’s top spy agency throughout their affair. Alice Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which smuggled an estimated $7 billion worth of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China.

Nvidia has denied that the company or Jensen Huang knew that Alice Huang was smuggling chips to China. Yet last year, Nvidia changed how it reported geographic sales, erasing Singapore as a separate category in its financial disclosures. The accounting change came after export controls were imposed banning sales into China, upon which sales to Singapore suddenly jumped by 72 percent, to $104 billion in 2025. Singapore was already known to reroute chips to buyers at other final destinations — where did the management at Nvidia think all those new chip sales were going?

Meanwhile, The Information reported that Jay Puri, Nvidia’s longtime sales chief, handled customer relations with Alice Huang, and also happens to be married to a former executive at yet another company being investigated for chip smuggling into China.

Even more shocking was the revelation, also reported by The Information , that Nvidia was responsible for introducing Megaspeed to Chinese tech giant Alibaba, which helped Alice Huang get bank loans to finance her purchases from Nvidia. Alibaba has ties to China’s military.

All together, it paints a picture in which Jensen Huang was not the dupe of a Chinese honeypot, but fully conscious of her scheme to allow China access to Nvidia’s chips. At best, Nvidia appears to have knowingly looked the other way.

This is a massive violation of our national security — the equivalent of allowing the smuggling of nuclear secrets into Russia during the Cold War.

Yet Nvidia did not operate alone in looking the other way. The company had help from the Trump administration.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rolled back restrictions against exports to China last spring, allowing Chinese AI companies to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips through cloud providers like Megaspeed.

Against the advice of many, Lutnick left Megaspeed off a list of companies barred from buying these most advanced chips for suspicion of smuggling them. Meanwhile, according to documents released by the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 800,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies — including companies controlled by the Chinese military. The documents also reveal “requests by Nvidia to depend on possible chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.”

The Commerce Department was supposed to be regulating Nvidia’s chips. Instead, it opened the floodgates to China and its military.

There was ample opposition within Trump’s Cabinet. Secretary of State Marco Rubio released a classified letter about the government’s suspicions that Alice Huang was a spy. Secretary of Treasury Scott Bessent raged at Lutnick over leaving Megaspeed off the entity list. Last week, many thought Lutnick would be fired. Yet despite all the reports of smuggling chips to China, Trump appears to have sided with Lutnick and Jensen Huang — and China — over Bessent and Rubio.

Trump’s reasoning isn’t a mystery: Just look at the stock market in the wake of the news of Jensen Huang’s return. As Trump posted to Truth Social in the wake of the news, “The country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy.”

Trump also responded to some of the concerns I’ve raised here. “The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security,” he wrote. “The attorney general of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”

Indeed: With so much help from Commerce, it’s possible that Huang’s highly dangerous leaking of chips to China broke no laws. But more disturbingly, it seems like the national security threat might be coming from inside the White House.

Batya Ungar Sargon is the host of “Batya!” which airs Saturday nights at 7 p.m. Eastern Time on NewsNation, the fastest-growing cable news network in the U.S. and a sister company of The Hill.

articles.title: Jensen Huang is back. Nvidia’s board still owes America answers
articles.summary: Nvidia restored Jensen Huang as CEO six days after the stock's worst week since 2008, but the foreign intelligence inquiry remains unfinished.
articles.body: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive on Nov. 12 after acknowledging an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. On Nov. 17, Nvidia’s chairman told investors that Huang would not return. Six days later, the board unanimously restored him as CEO and gave him back his board seat. Nvidia shares had fallen 23% the previous week, their worst week since 2008. They rose more than 31% in trading on Nov. 23 after the company announced his return. I suspect the selloff weighed heavily in that boardroom. So did the White House. President Donald Trump said Monday that he pressed the directors to bring Huang back and doubted they would have done so without him. The directors say they were satisfied with Huang’s candor and ability to lead and concluded, after receiving input from senior U.S. officials, that his return posed no national security risk. Candor is a curious word. Reuters reported that Huang misled Nvidia’s own general counsel about the nature of that relationship. RUBIO DUCKS QUESTIONS ON NVIDIA CEO'S REINSTATEMENT AFTER SOUNDING ALARM OVER SUSPECTED CHINESE SPY The directors also say their independent inquiry into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort will continue. What did they learn in those six days that made them comfortable restoring his authority before that inquiry was finished? Trump had good reason to want continuity at Nvidia. Huang co-founded the company in 1993 and built it into the leading supplier of AI processors. His return had support from billionaire Elon Musk and an online petition that drew more than 206,000 signatures. JENSEN HUANG'S NVIDIA RETURN SENDS CHINA A CLEAR MESSAGE: THE AI RACE IS ON Trump said the government had no reason to believe Huang’s reinstatement posed a national security risk, and he told CNBC that a "very thorough investigation" found Huang "did nothing wrong." The public has not seen that investigation. Eleven days earlier, Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department had reached no conclusion on whether the woman was a spy and that the FBI was investigating. And on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the administration was still seeking answers about Nvidia’s chip sales to China and who was in charge of export compliance. Those questions deserve answers no matter who runs Nvidia. JD VANCE SAYS HE AND TRUMP STILL 'DON'T KNOW' WHETHER ALICE HUANG WAS A CHINESE SPY As an Army inspector general, I investigated senior officials who used their positions for personal gain. Some cases involved affairs. The officials often seemed unaware of how much their staff knew or suspected. Word traveled well beyond the front office. When serious misconduct was substantiated, consequences mattered to the people who still had to work there. They were watching to see whether anyone in authority would act on what they had reported. That experience informs how I read the reports about Huang. Since I wrote about the affair on Nov. 10, news outlets have reported that he also had relationships with two Nvidia employees. If substantiated, those reports would give the directors more reason to examine his judgment and ask whether employees felt free to speak up. The foreign intelligence allegation raises a separate question: Did anyone gain access to sensitive information or restricted technology? FOREIGN SPY ‘HONEYTRAPS’ TARGETING AMERICA’S TECH ELITE SPARK ALARM AMID NVIDIA CEO SCANDAL The independent inquiry should establish what access, if any, resulted from the relationship. The company has also formed a committee of independent directors to oversee national security and export controls, and it is recruiting a chief compliance officer who will report to the board’s nominating and corporate governance committee. Employees need to know they can raise concerns about senior executives and have those concerns heard by someone with the authority to act. That compliance officer will work on the front line of a larger contest. In "The New AI Cold War," I argue that communist China is America’s principal competitor in artificial intelligence. Beijing wants access to American computing power now while building the capacity to do without it later. CHINA IS BUILDING AN AI WAR MACHINE. WASHINGTON MUST WAKE UP BEFORE IT’S TOO LATE Huawei, China’s technology champion, has published a roadmap for successive generations of AI chips that makes the ambition plain. As I wrote in October, nations that supply the systems others depend on gain influence that outlasts the sale. That is why deciding who gets advanced American chips is a national security decision. Trump said the government had no reason to believe Huang’s reinstatement posed a national security risk, and he told CNBC that a "very thorough investigation" found Huang "did nothing wrong." The public has not seen that investigation. The Trump administration has tried to preserve legitimate sales while tightening control over who can use the most sensitive American technology. In January, Commerce set conditions for reviewing sales of Nvidia’s H200 and comparable chips to China case by case. CHINA COULD EXPLOIT US TECHNOLOGY TO THREATEN AMERICAN FORCES, CONGRESSIONAL WATCHDOG LEADERS WARN On Nov. 16, Commerce issued a rule aimed at preventing restricted users from accessing advanced American computing through data centers in third countries. The rule’s value will depend on whether regulators and companies can verify who is using those systems. Nvidia’s importance cuts both ways. A serious disruption at the company would reach far beyond its shareholders. The board’s real question was whether the company could afford to wait for its own investigators. NOOSHEEN HASHEMI: AMERICA'S AI LEADERSHIP NEEDS MORE THAN ONE MAN The numbers say it could. Nvidia reported $65.3 billion in profit on $115.8 billion in revenue for the quarter ended Oct. 25, and its interim chief told investors the product roadmap was on track. I would have waited for the independent inquiry before returning Huang to the board and the chief executive’s office. Nvidia also needs a succession plan it can use under pressure, and Washington should want more than one dependable source of advanced computing. I returned Saturday from the Aurora Dialogues in Rome, where I took part in discussions on AI and security. I came home thinking about who can challenge a consequential decision when everyone is under pressure to move. At Nvidia, Congress now has the chance to ask. TRUMP OFFICIALS TOLD 'NOT TO STAB EACH OTHER' AMID DEMANDS NVIDIA DISPUTE BE PUT UNDER OATH IN CONGRESS Lawmakers in both parties criticized the reversal on Monday. Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, said the board acted "before Congress has even heard from him." Rep. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, said Congress needs to determine who approved sales of high-end chips to China. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Huang agreed to sit for a closed-door interview with three House committees on Dec. 1, and he has agreed to testify publicly before the Senate. Members should ask who at Nvidia can stop a chip sale on security grounds if the chief executive wants it to go ahead. They should finish the independent inquiry, disclose what they responsibly can and impose consequences if the findings warrant them, even if Wall Street would rather move on. articles.body: Joe Kasper, who served as chief of staff to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth during the early days of the Trump administration last year, has now said that Hegseth should resign. "Pete's ability to be effective has been constrained and very soon he’ll have lost any ability to be effective," Kasper said, according to Politico. "For that reason and others, it’s time for Pete to call it quits." "Pete's been belligerent in his stewardship of an office that will outlive him or any memory of his service," Kasper asserted, the report states. The outlet reported that Kasper suggested that Hegseth would not be able to work with the nation's legislature or obtain appropriate funds for department priorities. "He’s not just burned bridges up on the Hill," Kasper reportedly said. "He’s napalmed them. … He’s going to be suffocated, and it’s not like it’s going to be a slow suffocation. It’s going to be a quick asphyxiation." PENTAGON SUED BY THE INTERCEPT, FREEDOM OF THE PRESS FOUNDATION OVER ALLEGED 'BLACKLIST' OF NEWS OUTLETS According to Politico, Kasper noted that he understood within a week of joining the Pentagon that Hegseth's focus was "all about Pete rather than the institution and the men and women who support it." "There’s quite an emphasis on the showmanship," Kasper reportedly said. "The virtues of humility and basically service before self and those things have disappeared. I didn’t see those at the start, and see them ever less so now." The Pentagon chief "overindulged in ego, in attitude, and in entitlement," Kasper said, according to the report. He noted that he would rate Hegseth near the bottom 10% of defense secretaries in U.S. history, Politico reported. "I think history will be much crueler to him than I could be," he said. MASSIE'S PUSH TO IMPEACH HEGSETH SPLITS CONSTITUENTS IN HIS OWN BACKYARD: 'PURE SPITE' Due to an executive order that was issued last year, the administration now refers to the Defense Department as the Department of War and to Hegseth as the secretary of war. articles.title: China hawks clash with Trump over Huang’s return
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Trump faces backlash over Huang ▪ Army to proceed with Iowa detonation ▪ Group urges Rand Paul presidential run ▪ Nor’easter threatens Thanksgiving travel President Trump’s push to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia has drawn fierce backlash from China hawks in his party, who see Huang’s return as a potential…
articles.body:
▪ Group urges Rand Paul presidential run

▪ Nor’easter threatens Thanksgiving travel

President Trump ’s push to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia has drawn fierce backlash from China hawks in his party, who see Huang’s return as a potential national security risk and are calling for answers from all involved.

The president quickly took credit yesterday for his role in the leadership shake-up after Nvidia’s board of directors announced the unanimous decision to bring Huang back to the company, which led to a surge in the company’s stock.

“I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC . “I made the deal.”

Vice President Vance also touted his efforts on Huang’s behalf. Trump said he gave Nvidia’s board “assurances” that Huang posed no national security threat, and he cautioned that a scorned Huang might have gone to work for China directly.

“People say, is it a threat to have him?” Trump added in the interview. “No, it’s a threat to lose him.”

But China hawks who count themselves among Trump’s allies in Congress have broken with the president as he stands by Huang, who initially resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a Chinese tech executive suspected of spying for Beijing.

Huang is scheduled to testify in a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. He will also appear before three House committees in a closed-door hearing on Dec. 1.

Rep. Michael McCaul (R-Texas), a former chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, called on the Trump administration to provide information supporting the conclusion that there is no longer a national security threat.

“If administration officials now believe that Mr. Huang’s extramarital relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset — along with Nvidia’s deeply concerning sales of advanced chips to Megaspeed — no longer poses a national security threat, then they need to brief Congress immediately and release as much information as possible to the public,” McCaul wrote on the social platform X.

Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) said Congress “has much to investigate” and pledged to pass bipartisan chip export-control bills “one way or the other.”

“I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access ,” Cotton wrote on X. “ The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back.”

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) called for a full briefing on the scandal, saying , “This looks terrible on its face, and it drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang’s actions on our national security and economy,” Punchbowl News’s Andrew Desiderio reported .

“Ummm… she was, and is, a spy,” Rep. Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.) wrote on X. “How about we get serious about making sure China doesn’t steal US company technology? Or get serious about not selling it directly and indirectly?”

Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) said Nvidia bears the “legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws.”

“The risk of extortion by a Chinese asset who’s been banned by Singapore is risk enough to not rehire Huang. The worst part of this is what we may never know,” he added.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who sits on the Senate Banking Committee, wrote that Huang “ had multiple affairs including with subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy.”

“His own board described his behavior as lacking ‘candor.’ I’ve served on a public company board. His behavior does not support reinstatement,” the senator continued.

Former Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.), in a post on X, called on Congress to “ really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy. ”

On the other side of the aisle , House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) — who are poised to lead their respective chambers in the incoming Congress — pledged to investigate the administration and Nvidia executives for any wrongdoing and to work across the aisle on bipartisan legislation to “stop the flow of our most powerful technology to the Chinese military and other adversaries.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), who’s in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee next year, added, “ Why are Trump and [Commerce Secretary Howard ] Lutnick putting China’s interests first? Is it just the tens and hundreds of millions of dollars they’re making out in the open or does Huang have even more damning information on them?”

Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) accused the president of “selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f ‑‑‑ ing donation to his ballroom.”

Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif.) said he will resign from Congress on Dec. 1 after a House Ethics Committee report found “substantial evidence” of sexual misconduct. He said he recognizes the “seriousness” of the allegations but said he has “strong disagreement with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.”

Incoming House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) sent letters Monday to companies with ties to a venture capital firm linked to Donald Trump Jr., questioning whether they benefited from favorable treatment or insider access, NBC News reported . The companies include Polymarket, Juul, GrabAGun and Hadrian Automation.

Pennsylvania health officials confirmed the state’s ninth measles-related death this year, less than a week after the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years. The individual was unvaccinated and died after testing positive for the virus, the state officials said .

GO AHEAD: Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Monday night that the service would press ahead with plans to detonate lead-containing munitions in Iowa, despite alarm over the potential impact on local residents and the environment.

“It is the unanimous judgement of our people — the Army, Navy, EPA, ATF, FBI, DARPA, DoE, CDC, HHS, FEMA and every other agency involved — that the Army should proceed with an extensively mitigated, carefully controlled detonation, which will occur this Wednesday morning, as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions,” Telle wrote in a post on X .

Trump earlier in the day ordered the Army to halt the planned until both a federal appeals court and incoming Iowa Gov. Rob Sand (D) sign off on the plan to move forward.

Sand quickly threw the decision back to Trump, saying on X, “The Administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks.”

The incoming governor also said he asked the administration to share with the public the same information he has accessed in his briefings with the administration.

Environmental organizations have separately challenged the Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency permit for the Army’s action in court, but a three-judge panel for the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals yesterday denied the request .

DOUBLE WHAMMY: Virginia and Oregon are suing SpaceX, which acquired xAI in February, for allegedly creating and promoting artificial intelligence deepfake pornography and sexually explicit photos of children.

Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones (D) and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield (D) announced yesterday the separate lawsuits, both of which reference the company’s marketing of “Grok” as an AI companion with a “rebellious streak” that would “answer spicy questions that are rejected by most other AI systems.”

Jones specifically called out Grok Imagine’s “spicy mode” for allegedly allowing users to specifically create “nude and otherwise sexualized images” without obtaining consent. Rayfield said xAI “knowingly endangered kids and our communities” and “lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures.”

X Safety released a statement saying such content “has no place on X or in Grok” and that the company always acted quickly whenever “bad actors found ways to misuse Grok Imagine.”

articles.title: Newsom says Trump ‘doesn’t oppose mercy, he sells it’ amid commutation fight
articles.summary: Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) hit back at President Trump’s vow to challenge California’s commutation of sentences for some death row inmates, accusing the president of corruption and calling for reform. Trump, in remarks at the Department of Justice (DOJ) alongside victims’ families, called Newsom’s move “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country…
articles.body:
Gov. Gavin Newsom (D-Calif.) hit back at President Trump’s vow to challenge California’s commutation of sentences for some death row inmates, accusing the president of corruption and calling for reform.

Trump, in remarks at the Department of Justice (DOJ) alongside victims’ families, called Newsom’s move “one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen.”

The governor defended the policy in a social media video, comparing it to past comments and pardons from the president.

“To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That’s why every person, every person on California’s former death row will die in prison. No one walks out,” Newsom said in a video posted to social platform X.

He added, “Donald Trump’s criminals, they walk out.”

The Democrat has long been an advocate against the death penalty since taking office, issuing a moratorium on the use of capital punishment in 2019. Last week, he formally commuted the death sentences of all state inmates facing execution, changing their sentences to life without parole. California has not executed anyone since 2006.

Some saw Newsom’s efforts and response to Trump as a way to elevate a potential 2028 campaign , for which he is seen as a likely candidate.

Trump said his DOJ will fight Newsom’s efforts and called for legislation to strengthen use of the death penalty.

In a critical response, the governor accused the president of handing out pardons to his allies and the wealthy.

“No president can ever again turn the power of mercy into a business. No president and no one should be able to sell a pardon,” he said. “The Justice Department is not Donald Trump’s law firm. Justice is not for sale. Not in California, and not in America.”

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

Democrats have frequently blasted Trump for his use of the pardon or his suggestions about who else could receive one. On day one in office he pardoned more than a thousand people convicted of attacking the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. The president also pardoned the former president of Honduras, who had been convicted of trafficking cocaine into the U.S.

Trump recently suggested he would be open to pardoning tech billionaire Elon Musk after the midterms as he faces possible Democratic investigations. He also previously signaled he was open to pardoning Michael Cohen, his former attorney who was a key witness in the president’s New York hush money trial .

Presidents have been criticized for using their clemency power for allies. Former President Biden also shielded his son , Hunter Biden, from legal threats by pardoning him on his way out of office.

articles.title: How red Florida just weathered a blue hurricane
articles.summary: Florida has benefitted from its conservative legacy, and new residents are voting with their feet, coming here from other states.
articles.body:
The pundits have weighed in on this month’s election results, and the knives are out. It was a political bloodbath for the Republican Party as traditionally red states such as South Carolina and Kansas. The long-sought-after Texas turned blue, as did even Mississippi.

Meanwhile, Republicans watched as Georgia, Iowa and Arizona became bluer. Nine Senate seats and dozens of House seats have flipped to Democratic control.

Democratic Socialists of America candidates also secured seats across the country in both the House and the Senate. Although the media has dismissed their numbers as too small to warrant concern, the growing influence and increased vocal presence of the party’s progressive wing will undoubtedly demand an accounting from soon-to-be House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) and Senate Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.).

Yet as Democrats and progressive candidates celebrated victory after victory across the country, one state stood strong against the blue tsunami: the free state of Florida.

Like a lighthouse in the distance for distraught and disoriented conservatives — the Sunshine State defied the trends in this election. In fact, conservative Republicans swept all statewide races and maintained significant majorities in both houses of the state legislature. The margins were certainly closer than in Florida’s last two elections — as one would expect amid such a Democratic surge. But as the saying goes, close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades, and anything that stays above water in a flood tide is probably at a safe elevation.

So how did a diverse and rapidly growing state like Florida emerge with its conservative infrastructure relatively intact? The answer lies in the strange, sometimes boring world of policy, not necessarily politics.

Many states around the country have floundered under the weight of mediocre governance, but Florida has benefited from exceptional state leadership over the last eight years, with Governor Ron DeSantis at the helm, and a legislature, with some brief exceptions, generally working closely with him to advance courageous conservative policies that improve the lives of Floridians.

The Republican Party may have been dealt a devastating blow nationally, but in Florida “movement conservatism” triumphed.

Yes candidates, money, infrastructure and sweat equity matter in all campaigns. Governor-elect Byron Donalds (R) was an extremely strong candidate who ran a disciplined and thoughtful campaign focused on the needs of voters. What Florida voters said last week was that they by and large support what DeSantis has been doing and what Donalds is promising — courageous conservative policies. They want to keep the state’s zero income tax, universal school choice, tort reform and housing and insurance affordability. Florida voters said on Election Day, “More of this, please.”

The Sunshine State stands apart because voters understand that movement conservatism is not whatever it is they are trying in Washington, or most of the other supposedly red states around the country.

For example, in the face of declining student performance nationwide and parents demanding control over their children’s education, Florida crossed the finish line on universal school choice. Today, our state ranks number one in the nation for education freedom across multiple national benchmarks. When Floridians were hit with skyrocketing premiums and our property insurance market was teetering on collapse, Florida enacted reforms that are already proving very effective . Today, insurers are returning to the market , with several already announcing rate reductions.

And when property taxes became an increasingly pressing concern for homeowners, DeSantis challenged lawmakers and voters to pursue meaningful reform. Floridians responded by approving Amendment 3 with 62 percent of the vote. We are now on track to provide long-lasting property tax relief to Floridians, and Donalds has promised that more is to come.

These are not simply political talking points. They are examples of what happens when conservative leaders turn principles into policies that improve people’s lives.

For three decades, Florida has benefitted from this conservative legacy, and our many new residents are voting with their feet, coming here from other states. The incoming administration has promised to build upon that foundation with even bolder reforms.

What we learned last week is that Floridians, and most Americans, reward bold conservative leadership. But if conservative politicians instead deliver watered-down and weak-minded policies or crony capitalism — or, worst of all, do nothing — voters will look elsewhere. Across much of the country on Nov. 3, that’s exactly what they did.

Dr. Robert McClure is the President and CEO of the James Madison Institute in Tallahassee, Fla.

articles.title: Republican losses cloud Washington career path for conservative students
articles.summary: The new Congress, with its wide blue margins, is set to be a boon for Democratic staffers, liberal policy experts and interns seeking opportunities in Washington next year. But the next generation of conservative aides is looking warily at a Beltway job market already squeezed by economic pressures — and now further tightened by the…
articles.body:
The new Congress, with its wide blue margins, is set to be a boon for Democratic staffers, liberal policy experts and interns seeking opportunities in Washington next year. But the next generation of conservative aides is looking warily at a Beltway job market already squeezed by economic pressures — and now further tightened by the decimation of Republicans across the Capitol and an unpopular outgoing president.

Students and staff at the Republican Party’s traditional feeder institutions around the country say the election results were not all that surprising, but the margins have left their Washington-based job prospects looking more murky than before.

Matthew Purucker , a junior at Grove City College, a Christian liberal arts college in Pennsylvania that sends many students to D.C. as Republican staff and interns, said that while the election result was not unexpected to many on the staunchly conservative campus, the Democratic landslide may make it tougher for political science graduates to find a job they want, let alone one that will recognize their alma mater.

“I think Grove City is a pretty strong college for political science, but only for Republicans,” said Purucker, who is also the editor in chief of the student paper, the Collegian.

He emphasized, though, that students he talks to know politics is fickle and temporary, and the 2028 presidential and congressional elections have the potential to reshuffle job prospects back in their favor. But in the short term, the midterm result could sway some students to plan a future outside Washington.

“I’m sure seniors will be disappointed,” Purucker said. “If you’re hoping to work in D.C. with Republicans in leadership potentially, if you’re lucky enough to be able to get a job in that position, it’s definitely disappointing.”

Plus, D.C. is a city of connections and politics is a world of who you know. Small schools with deep Republican connections like Grove City and its counterparts around the country, like Hillsdale College in Michigan and Patrick Henry College in Virginia, are less likely to open doors in Democratic circles.

Ben Hodge , internship director at Patrick Henry, said he’s talking with students since the midterms about “different avenues to accomplish the same thing” in their careers, while encouraging them to be flexible in their future plans.

“We have students who then are just looking for other congressmen or senators, or think tanks, or maybe changing tactics a little bit to say, ‘Okay, I’m going to go work for a nonprofit or something,’” Hodge said. “Maybe they were going to work for a pro-life congressman, but now they’ll go work for a pro-life nonprofit because that’s an issue that they really care about.”

Patrick Henry, despite being an hour outside of D.C., doesn’t have the name recognition of, say, the University of Virginia or Georgetown. It also doesn’t have the relative neutrality: it regularly tops lists of the most conservative colleges in the U.S. and has been given high marks for its structure and leanings by groups like the Heritage Foundation .

Hodge said he’s found lots of success placing Patrick Henry students in internships, as many recruiters now are looking for what they call “mission fit” rather than a college’s name brand.

“There’s this perception that Trump Part One kind of took off the bench,” Hodge said. “And I think that at least the perception there is that that didn’t work out as well for him in his first administration, and that in the second administration, and for those types of things — and it filtered down to congressmen and women and senators’ offices — is that they’re looking much less for name brand and much more for mission fit. And I think that for those places where our students’ bona fides overlap, that’s actually worked out well for our students.”

Nonetheless, college students have plenty of reasons to be anxious about the job market in D.C, blue wave or not. One Hillsdale student said she hadn’t heard any concerns about the midterms affecting job prospects, but that the cost of living in D.C., Maryland and Virginia — and the general competitiveness of Beltway jobs — seem to be stronger worries for the many Hillsdale undergrads looking for their next steps.

“Hearing that there’s going to be fewer positions available, or that this application is going to be more competitive this year, something like that, I really just don’t think is going to discourage students from putting their best foot forward and trying, because we are a pretty competitive student body,” the student said.

It’s also possible that the resounding defeat of Trump-aligned candidates — and the loss of Republican power more generally — could embolden conservative donors and organizations, creating more opportunities for young talent who are tired of the Republican status quo.

Paul Glader , director of leadership programs at Advancing American Freedom, said he’s heard from college students on campuses around the country who are excited about a chance for the GOP to return to some form of traditional Reaganite conservatism, the philosophy that AAF espouses. Glader is leading AAF’s campus outreach and fellowship programs, hoping to bring even more young conservatives into the fold.

“You read these stories in Semafor, Politico about ‘groypers’ and people connecting to the new right or whatnot,” Glader said. “But from my vantage point, I’m meeting a lot of young people at colleges and in D.C. and beyond who want to connect to different principles, they want to connect to our brand of conservatism, which harkens back to Ronald Reagan, William F. Buckley, and others. They want to read Russell Kirk, and they want to hear from [former Vice President] Pence.”

Glader was at Grove City with Pence just last week, and he said he saw this kind of energy from students there.

“I think people are finally now starting to realize, well, two years from now is going to go very quickly, and the Republican Party and the conservative movement needs to really look and think about what just happened at the midterms,” Glader added. “I think there’s a real eagerness among younger generations to move beyond this era in Republican politics.”

Welcome to The Movement , a weekly newsletter looking at the influences and debates on the right in Washington. I’m Helen Huiskes, Senate reporter.

Send me tips, comments, and suggestions: hhuiskes@thehill.com

As the conservative movement and Republican Party examine their way forward in a post-Trump Washington, those on the center-right who felt sidelined by Trump’s rise are looking for a new champion. Some think they may have found one in retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.).

Bacon, who has been a congressman since 2017, and before that was a brigadier general in the Air Force, has said he is considering a run. At a recent gathering of “never-Trumper” groups in D.C., there was a lot of buzz about a potential Bacon candidacy, according to Chris Vance , executive director of Our Republican Legacy.

Bacon sent a prerecorded video to the gathering, and won over many of those present, including some people from Principles First, another center-right group. They like his background as a five-term congressman from a competitive district in the heartland, as a Bronze Star general, as well as his policy approaches.

“He might not run, and there might be other legacy Republicans who run, maybe, I don’t know. But he is exactly what our wing of the party wants to see in a presidential candidate,” Vance said. “I mean, he is absolutely opposed to the tariffs, absolutely opposed to appeasing Russia and Putin. He’s got the moral courage to speak out for a traditional Republican position on immigration, on other issues. I mean, right down the line, he’s with us.”

Vance said the midterm election’s “blue wave” means Republicans will be looking for a new way forward, which, he said, could be an opening for many in the party who have never liked Trump.

“I just think you’re going to see millions of Republicans snap back to what they were pre-Trump. I have never bought into this nonsense that the changes in the Republican Party are permanent. Nothing on this earth is permanent, particularly politics,” Vance said. “I think you’re going to see maybe everybody who runs try and move back towards a more Reaganite message.”

Bacon, for his part, told The Hill he’s “been talking” with the groups about a run, although he has yet to decide or announce anything.

“I have a message I’m passionate about, but I didn’t want it to be about me,” Bacon said. “I’m all about the message and vision. But it is possible I’ll be the only guy with a unifying message that we’ll need in 2028, and I should be prepared.”

Speaking of Republican presidential contenders, Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) keeps getting the question, and is making more noise. He has recently said he’s giving it “serious thought,” and he has also said his wife, Erin, is “trying to discourage it.” More here .

Several anti-abortion groups, including Americans United for Life, March for Life Action and Family Research Council, are out with a letter urging Trump to veto any legislation in the next Congress that restores Roe v. Wade or changes restrictions on federal funding for abortions. More here .

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) had to ask Republicans to show up for work after a string of absences derailed last week’s legislative agenda. Republicans have only a few more weeks in power, and the margins are so slim that Johnson needs virtually every Republican to be present to move bills. More here .

articles.title: Non merci: The ‘Arc de Trump’ and Shenzhen summit hit roadblocks
articles.summary: Trump has done nothing lately to be triumphant about.
articles.body:
Washington Federal Judge Tanya Chutkan last week extended her block on construction of President Trump’s planned United States Triumphal Arch, called the “Arc de Trump” by some, for an additional 14 days. Chutkan sided with local leaders, who argued the 250-tall structure would harm the community. We can breathe a sigh of relief.

Trump has done nothing lately to be triumphant about. His 90-minute Shenzhen summit with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping produced no major breakthroughs on the issues that mattered most.

Shenzhen hardly advanced peace in Ukraine, though the leaders said in a joint statement that they would “increase the production and supply of refined petroleum” — a hint that the U.S. might start lifting some of the energy sanctions imposed on Russia after Putin’s 2022 invasion. And Trump’s push to persuade Moscow and Beijing to reduce their nuclear arsenals yielded only an agreement to begin a dialogue. Iran was the elephant in the room, but there was no sign that anyone addressed it. And there was nothing new on Taiwan.

Xi was the big winner at the summit. When the three posed for photo ops, the optics were terrible in many of them for Trump, with the Chinese leader in the center and the two others by his side, like two planets revolving around the sun.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called it “Yalta 2.0,” a reference to the trilateral eight-day 1945 meeting attended by the U.S., Britain and Russia, in which the victors after World War II carved up Eastern Europe . Concessions to Stalin paved the way for decades of Soviet dominance in Eastern Europe and Northeast Asia, giving rise to the foreign policy shibboleth that if you aren’t at the table then you’re on the menu.

The Shenzhen summit, held at a secluded lakeside villa away from city center of China’s tech capital , not only burnished Xi’s role as a convener of global powers, but was also a personal victory.

As it happens, a half century ago, the Chinese Communist Party appointed Xi’s father, Xi Zhongxun, to be in charge of China’s southern Guangdong province. Shenzhen — then known as Bao’an County — was a mere waystation for transients fleeing China’s poverty for the neighboring British colony of Hong Kong. Xi Zhongxun encouraged foreign companies to set up factories, creating a dynamic tech hub virtually overnight.

Xi ran the table in Shenzhen. As a weakened lame duck Trump landed on the Shenzhen tarmac, a triumphant but straight-faced Xi was there to welcome him to the dynamic city his father had built. I learned as a lawyer in negotiation 101 that it is always better if they come to you.

The post-meeting joint declaration bristled with generalities. The New York Times headline read , “Trump Flaunts Camaraderie with Xi and Putin but Has Little to Show for It.”

Meanwhile, back at the arch, Chutkan ruled that work be stopped while she weighs legal arguments. On Nov. 5, she had originally halted work for two weeks minutes after the Trump administration signaled it was poised to begin construction.

The proposed arch has been savaged by architectural critics. Architectural expert Paul Goldberger has written that “Trump’s idea of classicism is not dignity and order but over-the-top gaudiness” and “super-size Las Vegas vulgarity.” The arch would be built in Memorial Circle, offensively close to Arlington National Cemetery.

The White House has argued the project is an overdue addition to Washington’s skyline. They contend that Congress’s decision in 1925 to authorize a pair of 166-foot-tall columns at the site had not expired, and that federal commissioners had discretion to change the design, providing a legal groundwork to move forward. The problem with their argument is that two 166-foot columns doth not a 250-foot arch make.

Three Vietnam War veterans, a historical preservationist, the District of Columbia government and the Commonwealth of Virginia sued to halt construction. The case is expected to follow a similar path as Trump’s White House ballroom — all the way to the Supreme Court which ruled 5 to 4 that the project could continue.

The Kennedy family also moved to intervene in the lawsuit , arguing desecration of JFK’s gravesite and other graves in Arlington Cemetery.

David Maloney, Washington’s historic preservation officer, warned last month that the arch would “severely damage an exceptional cultural landscape and one of the most important symbolic places in the nation.”

Trump has defended the project, noting that many other cities boast triumphal arches, but Washington does not. He also has compared his plans to the Arc de Triomphe , the 164-foot Parisian monument commissioned by Napoleon in 1806. The project is broadly unpopular. Polls say 57 percent of Americans oppose the arch, while 22 percent support the project. Some Democrats ran in the midterms in opposition to the arch.

Protesters also have regularly demonstrated at the site.

“I think it’s popular with the real people, not, you know, the paid protesters,” Trump said. “I think it’s very important.”

He failed to identify who the “real people” were. While Trump reportedly paid people to stand around him when he first announced his candidacy, I guess he can’t fathom citizens standing up for their aesthetic convictions unless there is a dollar under the rock.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Remote employees aren’t slacking — they’re surviving
articles.summary: The office debate keeps pretending that work happens in a certain place. But the evidence says something sharper: Work happens inside a day crowded by commuting, caregiving, household management, focus time and social connection — and exhaustion. That is why the finding by the Bureau of Labor Statistics that 35 percent of employed people did…
articles.body:
The office debate keeps pretending that work happens in a certain place. But the evidence says something sharper: Work happens inside a day crowded by commuting, caregiving, household management, focus time and social connection — and exhaustion.

That is why the finding by the Bureau of Labor Statistics that 35 percent of employed people did some or all of their work at home on working days should end the fantasy that remote work is a mere pandemic aftershock. Rather, it has become part of the ordinary architecture of American time.

The same report shows that 70 percent of employed people did some or all of their work at their workplace on working days, exhibiting a labor market that has settled into overlap rather than replacement. Leaders who still frame the choice as home versus office miss the operating reality: many employees now use both. This distinction should change how executives read office attendance.

Kastle Systems, which tracks access activity across 3,400 buildings and more than 60,000 businesses, reported that its latest 10-city Back to Work Barometer averaged 56.4 percent office occupancy during the week, while Tuesday peak occupancy reached 66.7 percent. That pattern suggests offices have recovered enough to matter, but not enough to restore the old five-day assumption. The office has become a coordination tool, not the default container for work.

The data also undercuts the lazy claim that flexibility equals indulgence. The Bureau of Labor Statistics shows, in Table 4, that full-time employees worked 8.1 hours on days they worked, with 8.5 hours on weekdays and 5.5 hours on weekend days. That means the flexible work argument does not rest on employees wanting to work less — it rests on employees wanting to place work inside a life that now has more visible constraints. Table 1 shows that 81 percent of people engaged in household activities on an average day, spending about two hours on them. Those hours do not disappear because a badge reader wants a cleaner attendance chart.

The gender data makes the leadership challenge more concrete. Table 6 found that employed women were more likely than employed men to do some or all of their work at home on working days — 38 percent versus 31 percent. The same release also found that women who did household activities spent 2.8 hours on them, compared with 2.1 hours for men. Leaders should not read those numbers as a reason to stigmatize women who work from home, but as a warning that rigid location policies often punish the people already carrying more unpaid coordination work.

None of this proves that fully remote work solves every problem, of course. A randomized experiment published in Nature found that a two-day hybrid work schedule improved job satisfaction and cut quit rates by one-third without damaging performance in a large technology company. The finding supports a practical middle ground: Use the office for collaboration, mentoring, trust-building and culture repair, while protecting home days for concentration and life logistics.

That middle ground also fits older causal evidence on why leaders should avoid universal claims. In a 2013 National Bureau of Economic Research working paper on a Chinese travel agency experiment, researchers found that call center employees assigned to work from home had higher performance and lower attrition — although some workers later chose to return to the office. Some people just perform better at home. Some need the office. Many need a predictable mix.

The biggest risk now comes from confusing compliance with productivity. A company can raise attendance and still damage performance if employees spend commute-heavy days on video calls they could have taken anywhere. It can lower attendance and still improve results if teams coordinate anchor days, redesign meetings and measure outcomes.

Executives should ask three hard questions. First, which tasks genuinely improve when people share a room? Second, which teams need synchronized office days rather than scattered attendance? And third, which employees face hidden time-costs that make rigid attendance especially expensive? Those questions turn flexible work from an ideological fight into an operating system.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics also points to a social problem that leaders should take seriously. People were less likely to engage in socializing and communicating on an average day in 2025 than in 2015, and they spent less time doing so. A recent report on research published in Science found that remote workers can experience deeper isolation , especially when they live alone. That new workday reality should push companies toward intentional connection, not blunt attendance quotas.

The next workplace advantage will go to leaders who manage time as carefully as they manage space. The best policy starts with the work, then chooses the location. The worst policy starts with the building, then forces the work to fit.

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators .”

articles.title: Cotton: ‘Congress has much to investigate’ after Trump push to reinstate Huang
articles.summary: Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) says “Congress has much to investigate” in the wake of President Trump’s push to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, something that caused the company’s stock to soar more than 30 percent Monday. “I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most…
articles.body:
Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) says “Congress has much to investigate” in the wake of President Trump’s push to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia, something that caused the company’s stock to soar more than 30 percent Monday.

“I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” Cotton posted on X.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president and CEO on Nov. 12 after media outlets reported he had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Megaspeed, who is alleged to have been in contact with a Chinese spy agency.

U.S. officials suspect Megaspeed, which purchased billions of dollars’ worth of advanced chips from Nvidia, may have circumvented export controls.

“Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip export-control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other,” Cotton wrote on social media.

Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3 and some Republicans have called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to also testify about the failure to step in earlier to ban chip sales to Megaspeed.

Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.), a member of the Senate Banking Committee, over the weekend suggested that the Commerce Department “knowingly” allowed Nvidia and Megaspeed to skirt export restrictions.

“It appears that they knowingly allowed this to happen. Scott Bessent has been saying, ‘Stop it.’ So I want to get both of them in front of a committee, put them under oath,” the Louisiana Republican said.

“Let’s answer some hard questions. And if Secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” he added.

The Commerce Department this week added Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, and several other Southeast Asian companies to a trade blacklist because of national security concerns.

articles.title: Trump to pardon Thanksgiving turkeys Freedom, Feathers
articles.summary: President Trump will honor a longstanding Thanksgiving tradition at the White House Tuesday by pardoning two turkeys fortunate enough to avoid ending up on the dinner table. Freedom and Feathers, two birds from Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, were selected by those who participated in an online poll last week to be pardoned by…
articles.body:
President Trump will honor a longstanding Thanksgiving tradition at the White House Tuesday by pardoning two turkeys fortunate enough to avoid ending up on the dinner table.

Freedom and Feathers, two birds from Deans Gap Farm in West Virginia, were selected by those who participated in an online poll last week to be pardoned by the president, the 79th presidential turkey pardon, according to the White House. Their patriotic names coincide with the U.S.’s 250th birthday.

Voters are able to weigh in on which of the two turkeys would be honored ceremonially in a poll on the White House website.

The two turkeys will retire to Texas A&M University in College Station, Texas, after receiving the presidential honor. The Texas A&M Aggies college football team will host a big rivalry matchup against the Texas Longhorns on Friday night, and the two turkeys could make an appearance, the National Turkey Federation told CBS News .

Both Freedom and Feathers received the first-class treatment offered to pardoned turkeys ahead of Thanksgiving, including a stay at a luxury hotel. An image released by the White House shows the pair of birds staying in beds at the Willard InterContinental Hotel in Washington.

Pardoning turkeys has a long history at the White House, but it was not formalized until President George H. W. Bush granted the first pardon in 1989. History dates back to President Abraham Lincoln, and the White House highlighted Presidents John F. Kennedy and Harry Truman setting birds free during their presidencies.

Trump has pardoned turkeys every year of his two presidencies, including last year’s pardons of Gobble and Waddle. At the 2025 pardon ceremony, Trump suggested that President Joe Biden’s turkey pardons were not valid because he used an autopen.

The president also quipped at last year’s ceremony that he almost named the turkeys Chuck and Nancy, after two of his top political targets, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

Tuesday’s turkey pardon ceremony is scheduled for 2 p.m. EST on the South Lawn of the White House, near the helipad.

articles.title: The lame duck Congress can give Indian Country long overdue truth and healing
articles.summary: The Truth and Healing Commission on Indian Boarding School Policies Act is a bicameral bill that has sat on the shelf for far too long.
articles.body:
It may seem trivial to some, but to Indian Country, federal reconciliation with the boarding school era remains a major milestone yet to be achieved.

Senate Bill 761, the Truth and Healing Commission on Indian Boarding School Policies Act , is a bicameral bill that has sat on the shelf for far too long, despite enjoying wide bipartisan support. The bill is backed by U.S. Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) in the Senate, and U.S. Reps. Tom Cole (R-Okla.) and Sharice Davids (D-Kan.) in the House, and it has an array of co-sponsors and supporters.

From 1819 to the 1970s, the U.S. government instituted a policy of removing tens of thousands of American Indian, Alaska Native and Native Hawaiian children from their families, placing them in more than 500 boarding schools throughout the country. At these schools, often administered by Christian churches, Native children were punished for speaking their language, forced into grueling manual labor, and suffered physical, emotional and sexual abuse. More than 973 deaths have been formally documented at these schools — all children.

Two years ago, former President Joe Biden issued a formal apology on behalf of the U.S. government for the abuses, calling the policy “a sin on our soul” and “one of the most horrific chapters in American history.”

President Biden acknowledged publicly what Native American families have always known happened behind closed doors in school halls and churches. We have carried this trauma for generations, yet little to no recognition of the impact it has had on Native American communities has ever been meaningfully acknowledged.

This bipartisan, bicameral proposal would establish a formal commission to investigate the complete history and continuing impact of these federal boarding school policies, creating a survivors’ subcommittee to guide the work of the appointed commission and affirming that the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act applies to items connected to these schools.

That means that all records related to the boarding school policies would be protected and returned to Native communities. In those documents, the truth survives, including enrollment files, death records and correspondence that families have sought for generations.

The commission would investigate, document and ultimately provide a set of policy recommendations to Congress to protect unmarked graves, support the repatriation of remains, provide formal aid in healing for survivors and descendants and stop this type of forced removal from ever happening again, including within the current foster care system.

Why now? Americans showed up in a massive way in the 2026 midterm elections in protest of government inaction and frustration with the current system. It was the largest election for Native American representatives, with more than 180 Native Americans winning local, state and federal seats, showing their power not just at the ballot box, but a strong desire for representation in their respective governments. They, along with all of Indian Country, demand action on issues important to us.

The push to get this bill signed into law is being led by the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition , a Native-led nonprofit organization led by one of us that has been working for decades to recover federal records, document abuses and help boarding school survivors and their families heal after decades of inaction and cover-ups.

The coalition has most recently been a partner to the federal government, as part of the former Department of Interior’s Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative , and has thus far collected and digitized thousands of records and stories to be archived in a permanent collection. The work is underway, but it must be formally recognized and funded.

That work is at risk if Congress doesn’t pass this important legislation, and time is running out for the survivors and communities that deserve to see justice and reconciliation in their lifetime. Many survivors are now in their 80s and 90s. Each year, we lose elders whose memories hold the answers families are still seeking. Every survivor deserves to see this work carried through in their lifetime.

In the 118th Congress, the bill passed the Senate with unanimous support but never received a hearing in the House. The bill, in its current form in the 119th Congress, features minor revisions to include more access to historic documents. There is no reason for the Senate and House to, once again, shelve this commonsense bipartisan bill that has already received wide bipartisan support.

During this time of transformational political change for our nation, we urge leaders in Congress to work together across the aisle to show the American people that progress is still possible, and that for Indian Country, this is no trivial issue — it’s of utmost importance and deserves to become law.

The time is now for Congress to pass the Truth and Healing Commission on Indian Boarding School Policies Act.

Deb Haaland (Pueblo of Laguna) is governor-elect of New Mexico. She served as the 54th U.S. secretary of the Interior and the first Native American Cabinet secretary. Nikki Santos (Coeur d’Alene Tribe) is chief executive officer of the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition.

articles.title: Gabriel Rufián responde al vídeo de Marcos Llorente dando de comer caviar a su hija: "Estos patriotas de pandereta pagarán más"
articles.standfirst: El contraste entre el lujo en redes y las carencias cotidianas tensa el debate
articles.summary: El contraste entre el lujo en redes y las carencias cotidianas tensa el debate
articles.body: El debate sobre los privilegios económicos y la desigualdad cotidiana ha vuelto a encenderse en redes sociales a raíz de una publicación de Marcos Llorente dándole de comer caviar a su hija. Lo que comenzó como una muestra de intimidad compartida ante miles de seguidores acabó convertido en el detonante de una discusión política de mayor alcance. El origen de la polémica estuvo en un vídeo difundido por el futbolista del Atlético de Madrid Marcos Llorente, en el que aparecía dando caviar a su hija en una escena cotidiana amenizada con música clásica. La imagen chocó de frente con las dificultades que atraviesan muchos hogares para cubrir necesidades básicas. Ante la repercusión de las imágenes, el candidato de Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya, Gabriel Rufián, replicó vinculando ese estilo de vida con la reclamación de una mayor contribución tributaria. En su intervención, resumió el reproche asegurando: "Lucharemos porque estos patriotas de pandereta paguen más". La frase condensa una crítica directa hacia quienes ostentan un alto nivel de vida o presumen de patriotismo mientras, a juicio del dirigente, no asumen un mayor esfuerzo fiscal para sostener lo común. Así, un gesto privado pasa a simbolizar una brecha social más amplia. La consigna internacional de Tax the rich (gravar a los ricos) se ha traducido en España en distintas propuestas electorales enfocadas en elevar la aportación fiscal de los grandes patrimonios y las rentas más altas. Por un lado, el PSOE ha planteado la creación de un nuevo impuesto específico para las fortunas que superen los 100 millones de euros —sin bonificaciones ni excepciones autonómicas— con el objetivo de recaudar unos 2.000 millones anuales destinados a vivienda protegida, pensiones y una prestación por crianza, además de sopesar una subida del tipo máximo marginal del IRPF para rentas superiores a 300.000 euros. A su izquierda, las propuestas amplían tanto la base de contribuyentes afectados como el alcance de los tributos sobre la acumulación de riqueza. Frente Amplio —la coalición heredera de Sumar— plantea un impuesto mínimo estatal del 2 % anual para patrimonios netos superiores al millón de euros y del 3 % a partir de los 50 millones, junto a un tipo marginal del 52 % en el IRPF desde los 300.000 euros y un tope máximo de 10 millones en las herencias (gravando al 100 % el exceso). Por su parte, Podemos apuesta por endurecer de forma escalonada el tramo estatal del IRPF a partir de los 60.000 euros anuales —alcanzando el 28,5 % estatal desde los 500.000 euros— y por equiparar la fiscalidad de las rentas del capital con la de los rendimientos del trabajo.

articles.title: Trump to award Giuliani Presidential Medal of Freedom
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is set to award former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday, honoring his public service and 9/11 leadership.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will award former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday during a closed-press ceremony at the White House, honoring the longtime prosecutor and "America's Mayor" for his lifetime of public service. The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the nation's highest civilian honor, alongside the Congressional Gold Medal, awarded to individuals who have made especially meritorious contributions to U.S. security, national interests, world peace, or significant public and private endeavors. "I am honored and humbled to receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom from my nation and from our Commander-in-Chief, President Donald J. Trump," Giuliani, 82, said in a statement. FOX NATION REVEALS HOW RUDY GIULIANI BROKE THE MAFIA'S GRIP ON NEW YORK Quoting his former boss, President Ronald Reagan, Giuliani added: "'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.' I share the credit with all the men and women who worked with me, disagreed with me, and loved me — particularly those who lost their lives in the causes we undertook together." White House assistant press secretary Olivia Wales praised Giuliani’s decades-long record in law enforcement and city leadership, noting that his work had "left a lasting impact on New York City and our Nation." "As U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Mayor Giuliani took down mob bosses and led a relentless war on crime," Wales said. "As Mayor, he transformed New York from a crime-ridden city into one of the safest big cities in the world, fostering economic opportunity and cultural greatness. And in the aftermath of the tragic September 11th attacks, he displayed strong American leadership in the face of evil."
